client_context: A 37-year-old middle school teacher who drinks every evening and occasionally comes to work hungover. A colleague noticed and expressed concern privately.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in — I know you mentioned you're between classes, so I'm not going to waste your time. No forms, no checklist. Just tell me what brought you here today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My wife. Basically. She... she said if I didn't talk to somebody she was done. Her words. So I'm here. I don't really think I need to be, but I'm here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came even though part of you doesn't think you need to. What's her concern — what does she see that has her worried?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She thinks I drink too much. Which — look, I drink. I come home, I have some beers, I unwind. I teach seventh graders all day long. Do you have any idea what that's like? I need something to decompress. That's not a disorder, that's just being an adult.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Middle school — that's a grind. And you've found that having a drink when you get home is how you come down from it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. I'm not out at bars, I'm not driving drunk, I'm home. I'm present — mostly. I'm not hurting anybody. And now suddenly there's this whole... thing. My wife's counting drinks, a colleague apparently said something to somebody, and I'm sitting in a wellness center like I'm some kind of... I don't know. It's a lot.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mostly present.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah, sometimes I fall asleep on the couch. But I'm exhausted. I'm up at six, I'm dealing with kids all day, I'm grading until midnight on Tuesdays. Of course I fall asleep. That's not — that's fatigue, not a drinking problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You used that word — mostly — and I don't want to make more of it than you mean. But I'm curious what the other part looks like. The part that isn't mostly.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...There was this one morning. A few weeks ago. I'd had — I don't know, more than usual. And I got to school and one of my students, she's a sharp kid, she said I smelled like something. And I told her it was mouthwash. It was. But. I don't know. That bothered me for a couple days.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That one stuck with you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Because kids — they notice everything, right? And I'm supposed to be somebody they can trust. That's literally the whole point. I've been doing this for twelve years and I've never... and for a second I thought, what are you doing? But then I got home and I just needed to not think about it anymore. So.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Being someone those kids can count on — that clearly matters to you. That's not nothing. Twelve years of showing up for them.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm good at my job. I am. Even my principal... look, I'm not falling apart here. I just — maybe the evenings have gotten a little heavier. Over time. My wife started keeping count and that's its own whole thing, but... I don't know. Maybe she's not totally wrong that it's more than it used to be.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're noticing it too — the mornings, what your student said, the evenings feeling heavier. What do you make of all that, when you're being honest with yourself?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...I think I've been using it as a crutch. God, I hate saying that out loud. But yeah. It's like the only part of the day that's just mine. No one needs anything from me for an hour. Nobody's asking for help, nobody's crying, nobody's failing anything. And I genuinely don't know how to have that without it anymore. Which is... I don't know what that is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me see if I'm hearing you right. You're not ready to put a label on this, and part of you is still pretty sure everyone's overreacting. And at the same time — quietly, in your own words just now — you're aware that something has shifted. The drinking is giving you something real: a space that's yours, a way to exhale. And there are also these moments — your student's comment, the mornings, your wife's worry — where you're starting to wonder if it's costing you something too.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. When you say it like that it sounds... yeah. I just — I don't want to be the guy with a drinking problem. I coach track. I'm a teacher. That's not who I am. I've worked really hard to not be that guy.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That identity — the teacher, the coach, the person who shows up — that matters to you. I want to ask you something and you can sit with it. Five years from now, when some of those seventh graders are out in the world somewhere, what do you want them to remember about you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Someone they could count on. Someone who actually saw them, you know? Not somebody who was just... half there. Going through the motions. That would kill me. That would really kill me.

client_context: A 29-year-old who moved to a new country alone and started drinking to cope with loneliness and cultural adjustment. Has no local support system.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for making time — I know you mentioned you're between classes. I'm Dr. Chen. I did get a brief note from your counselor at student services, but I'd much rather hear things in your own words. What made you decide to come in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She kind of pushed me to, honestly. I wasn't planning on it. I have a paper due at five so I can't stay long. I don't even know what I'm supposed to say. Like... I drink sometimes. That's basically the whole story.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So this wasn't really your call to be here, and you're not sure what you're walking into. That makes complete sense.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Everyone is acting like I have this huge problem. Back home nobody would say anything. People drink, it's normal. I moved here alone, I don't know anyone, so yeah, sometimes I drink at night. That's — I mean, what am I supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You moved here by yourself, and you've been navigating all of this alone. What has that actually been like — being here without your people around you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: "Adjusting."

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The way you said that — it doesn't sound like adjusting has been anything close to easy.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I go to class. I go home. That's it. For a year and a half. Back home you can't walk to the corner without running into three people you know. Here it's just... silence. And I didn't come here to talk about that, I came because she said I had to, so can we just — do you want me to say I have a drinking problem? Fine. I have a drinking problem. Are we done?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You said that with a lot of fire, and I'm not going to ask you to take it back. You're not here to perform a confession for me. I'm not interested in labeling you. What I am curious about — and you don't have to answer this the way you think I want — is what you actually want for yourself right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: What I want... I want to feel like a normal person again. I want to not dread going back to my apartment every evening. I... I didn't expect to say that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You want to feel like yourself again. And your apartment has become something to escape from, not somewhere to rest.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And the drinking is just... it takes the edge off when the quiet gets too loud. That's the only way I know how to say it. I know how that sounds. It's not like I'm sitting there with a bottle every night — it's more like, when it gets really bad, when I can't sleep and there's nobody to text... yeah. I reach for it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: "When the quiet gets too loud" — that's actually a really precise way to say it. I'm wondering, and you've clearly thought about this more than you let on — what would it look like to have something else to reach for in those moments?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've thought about it. There's an international student group on campus. I looked at the flyer like three times. But I always think... I'll show up and still feel like an outsider. And then it'll be worse somehow. But maybe... I don't know. Maybe that's not true.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've already been sitting with this idea. Three times. That's not someone who doesn't care — that's someone who's been quietly working on something even when it didn't feel like it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I do want things to be different. I just... I didn't think I'd be saying this between econ and psych class to someone I just met.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I've heard, and you tell me if it fits. You came here alone, and for a year and a half you've been pushing through without a real support system. Drinking has been a way to survive the hardest part of that — the silence, the loneliness. You didn't want to be told you have a problem. But underneath all of that, there's something in you that's been quietly reaching toward connection — looking at that flyer, showing up today. You want to feel at home again. Does that land?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... yeah. I didn't think of it all together like that but that's it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Given everything you just said — the group, wanting things to feel different — what feels like one small step you could actually take this week?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe actually go to that group. Not just look at the flyer. And... is it okay if I come back? Like, is that — can I book another session with you?

client_context: A 36-year-old veteran who started heavy drinking after deployment. Views drinking as normal military culture. Wife threatened divorce.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for getting on today, Marcus. I know this wasn't exactly your idea. What's your sense of why you're here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My wife set this up. Look, I'll be straight with you — I don't think I need to be here. She's got it in her head that I've got some kind of problem, and I guess... I don't know, I'm here to get her off my back. That's about it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came. Even when you didn't want to, even when it wasn't your call — you showed up. That tells me something about you, whether you'd frame it that way or not. So I'm not going to waste your time. You don't have a problem with alcohol — tell me what's actually going on in your life right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: What's going on. Yeah. I mean... I got back from my second deployment about three years ago. Things are just — it's a lot of adjusting, okay? I'm not sleeping great. My wife and I fight. I drink some beers at night to wind down, same as every guy I served with. That's not a problem, that's just how it is. You know what it's like over there? Nobody talks about feelings over there. You drink, you do your job, you come home. That's it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're carrying a lot — three years of trying to readjust, not sleeping, things with your wife feeling like they're fraying. And drinking is the thing that's been making that manageable. It worked over there, it's what everyone did, so why should coming home change any of that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Thank you. Like... nobody gets that. My wife, she grew up in this — her family's like, one glass of wine at Christmas, okay? She doesn't understand the culture. She sees me with a six-pack and it's like I'm some kind of... I don't know. Alcoholic or whatever. It's not like that. I'm not stumbling around. I go to work, I pay the bills. I'm functional.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've kept things running. Work, finances — you've held that together. And it sounds like part of what's frustrating is feeling like she's not seeing that, like she's only looking at one thing. What does she see that has her worried enough to threaten divorce?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She... okay, it's more than a six-pack sometimes. I'll admit that. Some nights it's more. And she says I'm... she says I'm not present. Like I'm there but I'm not there. And the kids — I've got two kids, seven and nine — she says I miss stuff. Like their games and school things because I'm... yeah. And one time I got pretty loud with her, which I'm not proud of. But I wasn't — I didn't touch her, I want to be clear about that. I just lost my temper.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took something to say. You're sitting here telling me — a stranger — that you got loud with your wife, that you've missed things with your kids, that some nights it goes past a six-pack. You didn't have to say any of that. What made you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't... I mean... she wasn't wrong. About the kids thing. My son had this — he was in a play at school, like a little thing, second grade. And I didn't make it. And he didn't say anything, he's a tough kid, but I could just see it on his face. And that... that bothered me. That bothered me a lot more than I let on.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your son's face stayed with you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it did. He doesn't complain, he's like me that way, just sort of... takes it. And I don't want him to have to take it. I don't want to be that guy. My dad was — look, that's a whole other thing. But I said I wasn't gonna be him. And lately I'm just... I don't know. I'm not so sure.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You made a promise to yourself a long time ago — that you'd be different from your dad. And right now that promise feels like it might be slipping. That's not a small thing to sit with.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. It's not. And I'm not — look, I'm not saying I've got a drinking problem. I still don't fully buy that. But I'm... maybe some things need to change. I don't know what that looks like. I don't want my wife to leave. I don't want my kids growing up the way I did. So... I don't know. Maybe I'm here for a real reason. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to make sure I'm hearing you right, because you've covered a lot of ground just now. You came in feeling like this wasn't necessary, that your wife was overreacting. But underneath that there's a man who's not sleeping, who's using alcohol to manage something that's been building since he came home, who missed his son's play and felt that more than he showed, and who made a promise to himself about what kind of father he'd be. Those things are all living in you at the same time.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
...

Yeah. That's... yeah. I don't — nobody's really laid it out like that before. That's a lot when you say it all together like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm not going to tell you what to do with it. But I'm curious — if things stayed exactly as they are, same pattern, another year from now. Where are you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Alone, probably. I mean... if she follows through on what she said. And I think she might. She's not — she doesn't make empty threats, that's not her. And the kids would be... they'd be with her, so. Yeah. That's not — I can't let that happen. I can't.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just said something important — "I can't let that happen." That's not someone who doesn't care. That's someone who knows what matters to him. I'd like to keep meeting with you, not to tell you drinking is the enemy, but to figure out together what's driving it and what you actually want your life to look like. Would you be willing to come back next week?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I'll — I can do that. I'm not promising anything crazy but... yeah. I'll come back.

client_context: A 42-year-old construction worker who drinks a six-pack every night. Referred by his doctor after abnormal liver tests. Thinks the doctor is overreacting.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Last time we talked, things were already pretty rough. You said you were going to try cutting back this week. How'd it actually go?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... it was a week. Look, my wife's the one who dragged me back in here, just so you know. I tried, okay? But we had a deadline on the site, crew was short two guys, and I come home and I just — I needed to wind down. That's not a crime. I don't see why everyone's acting like I'm some kind of alcoholic.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Short crew, deadline bearing down — coming home and needing to decompress made complete sense to you. And yet here you are again.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly. Everybody's got something, right? My buddy Mike smokes a pack a day, nobody's sending him to therapy. I just have a few beers after work. I've been doing this twenty years. The doctor's blowing this way out of proportion, I'm telling you.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Twenty years, and now the liver panels are coming back abnormal. What do you make of that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... I don't know. I looked it up, which I probably shouldn't have done. She said my enzyme levels were elevated — my liver — and I'm reading about this stuff online and it could mean a lot of things, right? Doesn't necessarily mean it's the drinking. Could be other stuff.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Part of you is hoping there's another explanation. And part of you read enough online to scare the hell out of yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well... my dad had liver problems. He passed when I was — he was 58. And I'm sitting there looking at this stuff and I'm 42, and I just... I don't want to go like that. I'm not saying it's the same thing. It's probably not the same thing. But yeah. It freaked me out a little, okay.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It takes something to sit with that kind of fear and still walk through that door. A lot of guys don't.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My wife... she cried. Not like dramatic or anything, just — we were talking about the results at the kitchen table and she just started crying quiet like. And my son Jake was right there, he's fourteen. And I just sat there. Didn't know what to say to either of them.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That moment hit different. Watching her cry. Jake sitting right there.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've worked hard my whole life to take care of them, you know? And I'm sitting there thinking — what if I'm the thing that blows it all up? Not some accident, not the economy, just me. Being stupid. And then this week I drank more, not less. Which I know. I know how that sounds.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me make sure I've got this right. You came back — your wife pushed you, but you came. The labs scared you more than you're letting on, especially with your dad's history. You tried to cut back and instead it got worse. And there's a part of you that's starting to wonder if the thing you've been using to cope could be the same thing that takes you away from Jake and your wife. That's a lot to be holding all at once.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. That's... yeah. When you put it all together like that I haven't really — I don't usually let myself think about it all at once like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A year from now — not best case, not worst — just a year from now. What do you want that to look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want my labs to come back normal. I want to not be thinking about a drink the second I walk off the job site. I want Jake to not have to worry about his dad. I'm not saying I can just stop cold — I don't know if I can do that — but I want it to be different than it is right now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're not asking for magic. You want a life where the drinking isn't running the show. And you were honest just now — you don't know if you can do this cold, but you know something has to shift. That clarity matters more than you think.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My foreman — he stopped drinking a few years back. I never asked him about it. I always figured it was a health thing or whatever. But maybe it was more like... this. He seems alright. He's solid. Maybe I could talk to him.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it take to have that conversation with him?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Probably just... asking. He's a straight shooter, he wouldn't make it into a whole thing. Maybe Friday after we shut the site down. Yeah. I think I could actually do that.

client_context: A 37-year-old middle school teacher who drinks every evening and occasionally comes to work hungover. A colleague noticed and expressed concern privately.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in. I'm Dr. Marcus — I work here at the health center. Can I get you anything, water, coffee? No rush. We can just get started whenever you're ready.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uh, no, I'm good. Thanks. I'm just... I'll be honest, I'm not really sure what I'm doing here. My friend kind of pushed me to come in. I don't usually — this isn't really something I do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What was that like, having your friend push you to do this?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, he means well. I know that. He's been my friend for like fifteen years so I'm not mad at him or anything. I just — I don't think he fully gets my situation. I've been under a ton of stress at work. Having a drink at the end of the day to unwind, that's... that's just normal. That's what people do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So on one hand you appreciate that he cares — and on the other, it feels like he might be misreading what's actually going on for you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. Like, I teach middle school. Thirty-two twelve-year-olds, every single day. Do you know what that's like? I come home completely hollowed out. So yeah, I have a scotch, maybe two, I watch something, I fall asleep on the couch sometimes. That's... I don't know, that's just how I decompress. It's not some big thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Teaching middle school is genuinely exhausting. I'm curious — what does a morning look like for you, the day after?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Most mornings are fine. I mean... most. Sometimes I wake up and my head's not great and I just kind of push through it. Coffee, get dressed, go in. It's fine. I'm functional. I've never — I've never missed a day because of it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You said most mornings. I wonder about the other ones.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...There was this one morning, maybe two months ago. One of my kids — he's a sweet kid, kind of quiet — he came up to me before class and asked if I was okay. Said I looked sick. And I told him I had a cold. But I knew. I knew exactly what it was. And I just... I thought about that for a while after.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That stayed with you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean — I don't know why that particular moment, you know? It happens, whatever. But that kid... he's the kind of kid who notices things. And I lied to him. And he looked at me like he was genuinely worried and I just... I'm his teacher. I'm supposed to be someone he can count on. I don't know. It felt bad.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Being someone they can count on — that sounds like it matters a lot to you. What does that actually look like, being that person for them?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It means being... present. Like actually in the room with them, not just physically there. And I've been doing this for eleven years and I love it, I genuinely love it, which is why — like, lately I've been wondering if I'm going through the motions. Some days I get to the end of the day and I can't even really remember what happened. And that scares me a little. I don't want to lose that. The part of me that actually cares about what I'm doing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just reflect back what I'm hearing, make sure I've got it right. You came in because someone who knows you well was worried enough to say something. Part of you thinks he's overreacting — and part of you remembers a morning that you can't quite shake. And underneath all of it is something you care about deeply: being genuinely present for these kids, because that's who you want to be. Does that sound right?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... when you lay it out like that it sounds more real than when it's just kind of floating around in my head. I don't love hearing it but... yeah. That's it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Not asking you to overhaul your whole life today. But I'm curious — if you imagined one small step, just one, toward being more of that person you're describing, what would it look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've thought about that, actually. Like, maybe just... not every night. Some nights I just don't. See what happens. I haven't really tried that in... I don't know how long. Which is, um — that's a little uncomfortable to say out loud. That I don't know if I can just not. But maybe I start there.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You walked in here not knowing what to expect, not sure you even belonged here — and you just said something that took real courage to say. That matters. Whatever comes next, that's a real starting point.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I don't know what happens from here but... I think I want to figure that out. Maybe come back. I actually think I want to come back.

client_context: A 20-year-old star athlete whose performance has been slipping due to partying. Coach gave an ultimatum. Torn between team loyalty and social life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for jumping on today - I know video sessions can feel a little off at first. There's no agenda I'm trying to push here. I just want to start simply: how are you feeling coming into this conversation?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Kind of pissed off. My girlfriend basically said she'd leave if I didn't do this, my coach is threatening my scholarship... so here I am. I don't even know what the point is. I don't have a drinking problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You didn't really choose to be here - that's coming through loud and clear. And honestly, that's a completely reasonable way to feel.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly. Like I put in 5 AM lifts, I give everything at practice, I'm out there every game no matter what. And then I go out on a Friday night and suddenly I'm the problem? Half my teammates do the exact same thing. It's just... it's not fair.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The double standard feels real - you're being held to a standard that doesn't seem to apply to everyone around you. I'm not here to argue that. Can I ask, what does a typical weekend actually look like for you? I'm just trying to understand what's happening.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, parties mostly. Drinks, shots, whatever. It's college, that's what people do. I'm not like... it's not like I'm doing anything crazy. I'm not drinking alone or whatever. Some nights maybe go a little longer than they should, but... my stats were fine until this semester and that's like a separate thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your numbers have slipped this semester. You brought that up yourself - what do you think is behind that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know... I've missed some practices. Told coach I was sick but I mean... and my reaction time's been off. I can feel it. But I can fix it if I want to. That's the thing - I could just stop tomorrow if I decided to.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You can feel it in your body - that's real self-awareness, and I don't want to skip past that. A lot of people in your position don't let themselves go there. I want to ask you something different though: what does football actually mean to you? Not the scholarship, not your coach - to you personally.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... I mean it's everything. I've been playing since I was like six. My dad played. I've got two younger brothers who come to every home game. The plan was always - it was always pro. That's been the plan forever. I don't know why you're asking me that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you've got football - your identity, your family, your future - and you've got the weekends, the parties, the release valve. Both of those are real. I'm just reflecting back what I'm hearing: those two things are starting to pull against each other.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. I mean, I know that. I'm not an idiot. I just - when Friday comes around I'm not thinking about any of that. It's like I turn that part of my brain off. And I guess that's the problem, right? I don't know. I hate that you're making sense right now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That thing you just described - turning part of your brain off on Fridays - what do you think that's actually about?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Stress, I think. Like... everything is so much all the time. Coach watching every rep, scouts supposedly looking at guys in my position, my girlfriend needs me present, my family is expecting... when I'm out I'm not that guy for a few hours. I'm just a person. But I wake up Saturday and I'm like... why did I do that. And then I do it again the next week. That's... that's kind of a bad sign, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to hold all of this together for a second. You came in today not really by choice, pretty frustrated about being here. But as we've talked, something else has been underneath all that: you can feel what's happening to your performance, you know exactly what's at stake, and you just told me you wake up Saturday wondering why you did it - and then the cycle repeats. That's a loop you're already aware of. Does that feel right?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... I haven't really put it all together like that before. Hearing it out loud is kind of... I don't want to lose football. Like genuinely. That would be - I don't even want to think about what that would do to me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If you were going to start protecting what matters most to you - even just one small move in that direction - what would that actually look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... maybe I don't have to be at every single thing. Like I could go out sometimes but actually decide beforehand how much I'm drinking instead of just going until I don't know what's happening. And I could actually talk to my girlfriend - really talk to her - instead of shutting her out. She's been way more patient than she should be. I think... I think I actually want to work on this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You walked in here frustrated and ready to write this whole thing off. And right now you just laid out a clear picture of what you actually care about and a real first step toward protecting it. That's not nothing - that's something to build on.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I think I just needed to say it to someone who wasn't gonna freak out or lecture me. I'm not saying this is gonna be easy but... I don't want to be the guy who had it all and threw it away. I want to still be playing five years from now. That guy exists. I just need to find him again.

client_context: A 21-year-old college senior who binge drinks every weekend. Friends staged an intervention but the student sees it as normal college behavior.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in. I'm Dr. Marcus. Take a seat wherever feels comfortable. So... what brought you in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uh, yeah. I don't really know, honestly. I saw like a flyer or something online about this place and I just... I don't know, I had some time before class so I figured whatever, I'd come check it out. It's not like there's a big reason or anything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something pulled you in here today. Even if you can't quite name it yet, that matters. What's been going on lately — just in general?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... it's senior year, it's stressful. My friends have been kind of on my case about stuff. They did this whole thing last weekend where they sat me down and were like, 'we're worried about you,' and it was just... it felt so dramatic. Like we're all doing the same stuff, you know? Everyone drinks on weekends. That's just college.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So your friends sat you down — that sounds like it was a lot to take in. What was that like for you, being on the receiving end of that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Embarrassing. Like... they made it this whole big deal. There were six of them. Six people sitting there staring at me like I'm some kind of... I don't know. And my roommate was crying, which was just — I didn't know what to do with that. I kinda just shut down. I didn't say much. And then afterward I just went to my room and I didn't really sleep.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That image stays with you — your roommate crying, all those faces. You didn't sleep. Some part of that landed.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean — yeah, okay, maybe. But it doesn't mean they're right. Like my roommate's always been kind of anxious and emotional about stuff, that's just how he is. And the others... half of them were drinking with me two Saturdays ago. So. I don't know what makes me the problem all of a sudden.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It feels unfair. Like you're being singled out for something everyone's doing. And at the same time, you're here. I'm curious — if your friends are wrong, what would it mean if they were even a little bit right?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
...

I don't want to think about that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's okay. You don't have to. You've already sat with more than most people would today just by walking through that door.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess. I just... I feel like if I admit that anything's wrong, then that makes me like — an alcoholic or something. And that's not who I am. I'm a good student. I've got a 3.4 GPA. I'm graduating in May. I'm not like, stumbling to class or whatever. So.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've worked hard. You've kept things together. And you're also carrying this fear that acknowledging something might mean losing the story you have about yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, exactly. Because if my friends are right then... what does that say about the last three years? Like every weekend, every party, every — I built my whole social life around this stuff. If that's the problem then I don't even know who I am without it. And that sounds so stupid to say out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound stupid at all. That's actually one of the most honest things anyone's said to me in a while. You're not just talking about drinking — you're talking about identity. Who you've been. Who you might be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I don't know. Maybe. I've just been really tired lately. Not like sleepy-tired. Just like... tired of waking up on Sundays feeling like garbage and not remembering parts of the night and then checking my phone and kind of dreading what I texted people. That happens a lot. More than it used to.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me make sure I'm hearing you right. You came in today not totally sure why. Your friends did something that felt embarrassing and unfair, but it didn't fully leave you. You've been tired — not physically, but something deeper. And you're starting to notice a gap between the guy who has a 3.4 GPA and is graduating in May, and what Sunday mornings actually feel like. That's a lot to be holding.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you put it like that it sounds... yeah. It sounds worse than I've been letting myself think about it. I don't know. I still don't think I'm like — I still think my friends overreacted. But like... I don't know, maybe there's something there. I'm not saying they're right. I'm just saying maybe I've been kind of on autopilot and I haven't really looked at it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's not a small thing to say. What would it look like to start looking at it — just a little, at your own pace?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe... like maybe talking to someone? Not in a group or whatever, that sounds awful. But like this, I guess. I'm not making any promises. And I'm still not convinced I have a problem. But I could... I mean, I'm here. I could come back.

client_context: A 20-year-old star athlete whose performance has been slipping due to partying. Coach gave an ultimatum. Torn between team loyalty and social life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, good to see you again. Last time we talked things were actually starting to look up a little — and then you mentioned in your message that this week hit differently. I just want to start by saying, there's no judgment here. How are you doing today, really?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... honestly? Not great. My friend basically ambushed me into coming back here in the first place, and now it feels like everyone's just — like, my coach, my friends, you — everyone's got an opinion on what I'm doing with my life. It's a lot.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It feels like you've got people coming at you from every direction.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. And like — I had one bad weekend, okay? One. And suddenly it's this whole... thing. My coach pulls me into his office, my teammate texts my other friend, and now I'm here again. It's like — I'm not some addict or whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You want people to see the full picture — not just zoom in on one weekend.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Right. I work my ass off — sorry — I work really hard. Like, you know how many five AM practices I've done this semester? And my GPA is still decent. One party weekend and suddenly I'm the problem. That doesn't feel fair.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's a real sense of injustice there — like all that effort isn't being seen. And at the same time, I'm wondering... and you don't have to answer this right now... what was it about this past weekend that felt different, even to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... I don't know. It just got out of hand faster than I expected. I wasn't trying for it to go that far. I was just trying to unwind, you know? Like everyone else does. But I woke up Sunday and I had three missed calls from my coach and I just... I felt sick.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something about that Sunday morning felt different.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Like, I've partied before and brushed it off no problem. But this time I kept thinking about the game on Friday. I fumbled twice. And I kept replaying it and I couldn't tell — was it the drinking, or was I just off? I don't know. That... that scared me a little.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That uncertainty — not being able to tell if it's affecting your game — that's been sitting with you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It is. Because football is... I mean, that's everything to me. Like my whole life I've worked for this. The scholarship, the team, maybe — I don't know, maybe something after college if things go right. And I'm not trying to throw that away. It just kind of... happens.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Football isn't just a sport for you — it's tied up in who you are, your future, your sense of yourself. And there's a part of you that's worried the drinking might be quietly getting in the way of all that, even when you're not trying to let it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And that's... it's hard to say out loud. Because if I admit that, then what — I'm like, admitting I have a problem? And I don't... I mean, I don't think I have a problem. But maybe I don't have it as controlled as I thought I did. I don't know, man.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That takes real honesty to sit with. What would it look like — for you — to feel like you were actually back in control? Not what your coach wants, not what your friend wants. What would that feel like to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I think I'd just feel like myself again. Sharp. Ready. Not dreading practice or checking my phone worried there's another voicemail. Just playing the way I know I can play. I know what that feels like. I just haven't felt it in a while.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull a few things together, if that's okay. You came in today feeling like people were piling on — and that frustration is completely real. But underneath it, you've been carrying something heavier: this worry that drinking might be quietly costing you the thing that matters most to you. Football. Your performance. Who you want to be. And there's a part of you — maybe a bigger part than you've said out loud before — that wants to feel sharp and in control again. Does that sound about right?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's pretty much it. I don't want to be the guy who had all this potential and just — you know. I've seen that happen to people. I really don't want to be that guy.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You know what you don't want. What's one small thing — nothing huge, just one thing — that you feel like you could actually do this week that would move you even a little bit toward that version of yourself?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I think just... not drinking before Thursday's practice. Just that. See how I feel on the field. Because I think I already know the answer — I just need to prove it to myself.

client_context: A 20-year-old star athlete whose performance has been slipping due to partying. Coach gave an ultimatum. Torn between team loyalty and social life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey Marcus, glad you could make it. I know telehealth is a little weird at first — you can be wherever you're comfortable, no pressure. So your friend set this up. What's your take on being here today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I'm here, right? Jake kind of freaked out and set the whole thing up, and I didn't want to make it into a bigger deal by just not showing. But honestly? I think he overreacted. Like, I appreciate that he cares, but I don't really think I have a problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you're here partly for Jake. Not necessarily because you think something needs to change.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, basically. I drink on weekends, same as everyone else on the team. More than some guys, sure, but... I don't know. Coach has been on my ass lately and I think everyone just kind of piled on after that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me more about what's been going on with your coach.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: He, uh... he called me in last week. Said if my times don't come back up by regionals he's pulling me from the relay. Which is — that's never happened. I've been first leg since freshman year. And he basically implied it was the partying that was doing it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a lot to carry. You've built something real over three years, and now it feels like it's suddenly at risk.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. Okay, but like — I've been stressed, and going out is how I decompress. After a brutal week of doubles you just need to let loose. It's not like I'm showing up to meets drunk or whatever. I know where the line is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That need to decompress makes total sense — athletes carry a lot and you have to put it somewhere. I'm curious though... what does that relay spot actually mean to you? Like, past just the starting position.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... it's everything, man. My dad swam in college too, never made it to regionals. I've been to regionals three times. He drives four hours to every home meet. It's — I don't know. It's not just swimming.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So on one side there's the parties — the release valve, your social world. And on the other there's everything you've worked toward, what you're building, what it means to your dad. And those two things are starting to pull against each other.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I hadn't really put it like that. It's weird because — okay this is gonna sound dumb — but I'll be at a party on Thursday night and I'm thinking about Saturday's workout the whole time anyway. Like I can't even fully enjoy it anymore.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That doesn't sound dumb at all. You just named something important — it's not even giving you what you're going there for.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Huh. I mean... yeah. I go out because it's supposed to be a break, but it's not really a break. It's just more stress with a hangover on top. I've been telling myself it helps but... I don't know if it actually does.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just check that I'm tracking this right. You came in today mostly to keep the peace — didn't really see a problem. But as we've been talking, a few things have come into focus: your relay spot is genuinely on the line, your coach said it directly, and now you're recognizing that the drinking isn't even doing what you need it to do anymore. That about right?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. That's... pretty much it. I think I've been telling myself it's fine for a while because it's easier than actually dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it look like — for you — if things were actually going the way you wanted them to by the time regionals comes around?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I'd be back in the water feeling like myself. Not dragging through practices. I want my dad to see me compete this year, not wonder what happened to his kid. I think I just... I need to figure out what I actually need to decompress instead of just defaulting to going out.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You walked in here today for Jake. But somewhere in this conversation, you started talking about what you want. That's not a small thing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I think I needed to hear myself say some of this out loud. I'm not gonna pretend I have it all figured out, but — this is the first time it's felt like something I actually have some control over. Like I have a choice here.

client_context: A 20-year-old star athlete whose performance has been slipping due to partying. Coach gave an ultimatum. Torn between team loyalty and social life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in. I'm Dr. Reyes — or just Marcus, whatever works for you. So, fair warning, this place looks way more intimidating than it actually is. Can I ask what brings you in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uh, yeah. My doctor like... she said I should come in. I don't really know what this is supposed to be, honestly. Like am I in trouble or something? I feel like I got sent to the principal's office.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Ha — okay, I get that. And for the record, I'm a terrible principal. No detention here. This is just... a conversation. Nothing you say leaves this room, no one's grading you. I'm just curious about you. What did your doctor tell you this was about?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She mentioned, um... drinking. Which, I mean — I'm in college. Like everyone drinks. I don't see why I specifically got flagged for that, it's not like I'm some... I don't know. It's fine. I just party on weekends.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So on one level, it feels pretty normal — college, weekends, everyone's doing it. And at the same time, something got you here today. I'm wondering if there's maybe a little more going on under the surface.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. My coach kind of got in my face last week. Said my times are slipping and I look like I haven't slept in a month, which... okay, fair. But it's not just the drinking, there's a lot going on with school and the team and... I don't know. It's complicated.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds like a lot of pressure landing on you all at once. Coach on your case, school, the team... and it sounds like you actually care about your performance — like that comment about your times, that landed.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, it did. I've been running since I was nine. Like... swimming is the one thing I'm actually good at, you know? And I've worked so hard to get here and now I'm just... watching it kind of fall apart and I don't even know how it happened. That's the messed up part.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Eleven years of swimming. That's not a hobby, that's who you are. And now there's this gap between the person you know yourself to be and what's actually showing up in the water. What do you make of that gap?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? It scares me. Like I keep telling myself I'll dial it back after this weekend, or after finals, there's always a reason. And I know that sounds like... I know how it sounds. But the guys on the team, that's my whole social life. If I stop going out with them I'm just... alone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So there's real fear on both sides — fear of losing your edge in the water, and fear of losing your connection to the people you're closest to. That's not a small thing. You're trying to hold onto both and it sounds like right now the cost is pretty high.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, exactly. And like... my coach basically said if I don't get it together by regionals I'm off the relay team. Which is — that would kill me. The relay is everything. But I also don't want to be the guy who like, bails on everyone and sits alone in his room.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to reflect something back to you and tell me if I'm off base. It sounds like you're not really here because your doctor referred you. You're here because part of you already knows something needs to change — and you're trying to figure out if that's actually possible without losing everything else.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I guess that's right. I didn't think about it that way but... yeah. I want to fix it. I just don't really know what fixing it looks like.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's actually a really honest thing to say, and I don't think most people walk in here and say it that clearly. You've named the problem, you see the cost, and you're not pretending it's all fine. That takes guts. So — if you imagine a version of yourself that's back in form, competing well, and still has that connection with your teammates... what does that look like? Is that a realistic picture for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think so? Like I don't think I have to completely disappear from everything. Maybe I just... show up to stuff and don't always drink? I don't know if that's actually possible with this group but... maybe. Some of them care more about swimming than they let on. Like, we all do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me pull together what I'm hearing. You've got eleven years in the sport, it's core to who you are. Lately the drinking has been filling a real social need but it's coming at a cost — your performance, your standing with your coach, maybe your own sense of self. And what you're starting to see is that changing your relationship with drinking doesn't necessarily mean blowing up your friendships. It might actually be something your teammates could get behind too.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. That's... yeah. When you say it like that it sounds more doable than it did when I walked in. I was honestly expecting you to like, hand me a pamphlet and tell me I'm an alcoholic.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Ha — I'm fresh out of pamphlets. But seriously, I'm glad it feels more workable. You came in here not knowing what to expect and you just did a lot of honest thinking. That matters. What feels like one small thing you could try before we meet again — something that's actually yours, not something your coach is demanding?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe just... not drinking at the next team thing. Just to see what happens. See if anyone even notices. I think I've been using it as like, a social crutch more than I realized. I want to at least try.

client_context: A 72-year-old with chronic pain who has been mixing alcohol with pain medication. Family is terrified. Doesn't want to burden anyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Come on in, have a seat wherever you're comfortable. I'm glad you made it in today. I know the last few days have probably been a lot.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Thank you. I... yes, it has been. The hospital was... well. I don't usually do things like this. Come to places like this. My daughter drove me, she's waiting out there, which I feel terrible about. She has work.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She wanted to be here with you. That says something. And you came — that takes something too, especially after everything you just went through. What was it like, the past few days?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Frightening, honestly. I woke up on the kitchen floor and I didn't... I couldn't tell you how long I'd been there. My hip was just screaming. And then the ambulance, and my daughter's face when she got to the hospital — I don't want to think about that face. She was so scared. I scared her.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're carrying that — her fear, on top of your own. That's a heavy thing to hold.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've been a burden my whole life trying not to be a burden, if that makes any sense. My husband passed four years ago and I just... I manage. I've always managed. But the pain lately, it's — some nights it's just relentless. The hip, the arthritis in my hands. And the pills they give me, they help some, but not enough. Not at two in the morning.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Two in the morning is its own kind of alone. And you found something that got you through those nights.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: A glass of wine. Sometimes two. I know how that sounds. I'm not — I'm not a drinker, I want you to understand that. My mother was, and I swore I never would be. But it just... it took the edge off. And then it was taking the edge off along with the Percocet and I suppose I stopped paying attention to how much of both I was having.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've seen what alcohol can do to a life up close, with your mother, and you've spent years being careful about that. And here you are anyway, and that probably feels like a particular kind of loss.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yes. It does. I never thought — I'm seventy-two years old. I thought I was past the age of this kind of thing happening to me. Stupid, maybe.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Not stupid. Pain has a way of narrowing our options down to whatever works, even when part of us knows the cost. You mentioned you've talked to someone before — counselors. What was that like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: They were fine, I suppose. One of them was very young. Nice enough girl. But I always felt like I was... performing, somehow. Saying the right things. And then going home and nothing was different. The pain was still there. Harold was still gone. I don't know what I expected them to do about any of that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You showed up, said what you thought was expected, and still went home to the same pain and the same empty house. That's exhausting. And here you are trying again anyway.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My daughter asked me to. And I... I don't want to end up back on that kitchen floor. Or worse. I'm not ready for worse.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That matters — that you're not ready for worse. I want to make sure I understand what you're up against. You're dealing with real, serious pain that isn't being managed well enough, and the alcohol has been filling that gap. Would it be alright if I shared a bit about what I've seen help in situations like yours?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The mixing of alcohol and opioids is genuinely dangerous — your body can forget to breathe. That's likely what happened on that floor. But here's what I also know: the pain is real, the loneliness at two in the morning is real, and we can't just take something away without putting something better in its place. What I'd like to do is work with you and your doctor together, so we're actually treating the pain differently, and find you something for those nights that isn't going to land you back in the ER.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That... that would be something. No one's ever said it quite like that before. Like the pain was the real problem. They usually just tell me not to drink.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing, make sure I've got it right. You came in today because you scared yourself and you scared your daughter, and you don't want that to happen again. You've been trying to manage serious pain on your own for a long time, mostly at night, and the wine became part of that. You've tried talking to people before and it didn't quite fit. But you're here now, you're open to something different, and you want to actually have the pain addressed — not just be told to stop. Does that sound like you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That sounds exactly like me. I didn't expect you to... yes. That's exactly right.

client_context: A 50-year-old who was sober for 3 years but relapsed after a sudden job loss. Feels deep shame and hopelessness. Has been to AA before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you today. I know last week was really hard. How are you doing coming in here today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm... I don't know. I'm here. That's about the best I can say. I drank again on Thursday. You probably already know that from my check-in.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You showed up today even after a really painful week. That matters.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Does it? I mean... three years. Three years I had. And now it's just... gone. I feel like such an idiot. Like I should know better by now, I'm fifty years old for God's sake.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The shame is hitting really hard right now. Can you tell me a little about what Thursday looked like — what was going on before you picked up?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I got another rejection email. From that logistics company. That was the fourth one in... I don't know, six weeks? And I just — I sat there in my kitchen, and it was like, what is the point. What is the actual point. And I had some beers my son left in the fridge from when he visited and... yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you were already carrying weeks of rejection, and that fourth email just became too much to hold alone in that moment.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's exactly it. And the thing is, I know what I was supposed to do. Call my sponsor. Go to a meeting. I know the drill. I've done it a hundred times. I just... I didn't. I didn't want to hear it. I didn't want to sit in a circle and say my name and have people look at me like I failed.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like the shame of possibly relapsing actually got in the way of the thing that might have helped prevent it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Huh. I never thought about it like that but... yeah. Yeah, that's kind of messed up, isn't it. I was already so scared of what people would think that I just — I dug the hole myself. God.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a really significant thing you just noticed. I want to stay with that for a second and also ask — when you were sober those three years, what did that time mean to you? What was different about your life?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I was... present. Like, my daughter got married in 2023 and I was actually there, you know? Not checked out, not counting down till I could leave and get a drink. I was just there. I danced with her. I remember all of it. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Being present for your daughter's wedding — fully there, remembering all of it. That's what sobriety gave you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: And she's... she's pregnant now. First grandkid. Due in October. And I keep thinking — what kind of grandfather am I going to be? The drunk one? No. No, I don't want that. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think it's important. You relapsed after a brutal stretch of rejection and real loss — that's real, that happened. And at the same time, you came back here. You connected Thursday to loneliness and shame, not to who you fundamentally are. And you just talked about your daughter, your grandchild coming in October — and you were clear: you don't want to be the drunk grandfather. That's not just words. That's you knowing exactly what you're fighting for.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you put it like that... I don't know, it doesn't feel completely hopeless. Which is not how I felt walking in here, so. That's something I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've done this before — you know how to get back. What feels like a first step you could actually see yourself taking this week?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: There's a Thursday night meeting, the one I used to go to before... before all this. I know people there. Real people who aren't going to judge me for coming back. I think I could go to that. I think I could do that one thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Three years didn't disappear on Thursday. You built that. You know how to do this, and you know why it matters to you. Walking back into that room this Thursday — that's not starting over. That's picking it back up.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, okay. I can do Thursday. I'll go Thursday.

client_context: A 40-year-old single parent who has been drinking a bottle of wine nightly to cope with the stress of raising two kids alone. Knows it's too much but feels trapped.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So, I know you're not exactly here by choice — sounds like your friend kind of... nudged you in the door. How are you feeling about being here today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I think she overreacted. I'm fine. I've just been a little stressed lately and she kind of made it into this whole... thing. I don't really know why I'm here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A little stressed. And yet someone who cares about you cared enough to make it a whole thing. That says something — about her, but maybe also about what she's been seeing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, yeah, but — look, I hold down a job, my kids are fed, they go to school, they're in activities. I am not falling apart. I just — I have a glass of wine at the end of the day like every other adult in America.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're holding it all together — solo, two kids, full-time job. That's a lot of plates spinning. What does the end of one of those days actually look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I come home, I make dinner, help with homework, get them to bed... and then I open a bottle of wine and I watch TV. That's it. That's — that's my decompression time. It's the one hour that's just mine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That one hour is everything. And the wine helps your brain stop doing... whatever it's doing all day.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. I can't just — I can't sit there with my thoughts. They're... it's a lot. And yeah, I go through the whole bottle, but it's not like I'm getting drunk-drunk. I'm not slurring or anything. I'm just... turning it off.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That is a very busy brain you've got. [slight smile] Can I ask — what happens on the nights you try not to open it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...I don't really try. [pause] I mean — I did once. Like a month ago. I just sat there and I could not sleep. I was running through the electric bill, my son's parent-teacher thing, whether my ex is actually going to show up this weekend... it was awful. I poured one eventually anyway.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You tried. That took something — even once. And when you describe sitting with all of that... it sounds less like wanting a drink and more like there's nowhere else to put everything.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [quiet] Yeah, that's... that's actually a pretty good way to put it. I don't have anyone to hand it off to at the end of the day. It all just stays with me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What's the thing underneath all of it — not the bills, not your ex — what's the deeper worry you're trying not to sit with?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...[long pause] That I'm not doing a good enough job. With them. My kids. I'm there, I show up, but I'm so tired and then by 9pm I'm just... zoned out. My daughter's been asking me to read with her and I keep saying I'm tired. I mean I am, but... that's not — that's not what I wanted it to look like.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you came in here pretty sure everything was fine. And somewhere between then and now, you've named the one thing a bottle of wine can't actually fix — which is this fear that you're slowly missing them. I want to make sure I'm hearing that right.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. [exhales] Yeah. It keeps me up some nights. Which is — kind of ironic, right? The thing I use to sleep is now keeping me awake worrying about using it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If the wine just... vanished — no withdrawal, no cravings, magic wand — what would you actually do with that 9pm hour?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'd... I used to love reading. Before everything fell apart. I'd probably do that. Or maybe — I don't know — actually sit with my daughter for once instead of telling her tomorrow. [small laugh] That sounds nice actually. When I say it out loud it sounds really nice.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You walked in here ready to tell me there was no problem. And by the end you just described exactly the life you want — and you're the one who put it there. That's not me, that's you. We can figure out how to get there, but that part? That's already yours.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I do want it. I just... I'm scared, honestly. Like what if I stop and I feel everything and I can't handle it? What if I'm worse without it? [pause] But I guess I don't really know that yet.

client_context: A 31-year-old new mother who has been drinking wine nightly since the baby was born to cope with postpartum stress. Partner is supportive but worried.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came back. [pause] That takes something — especially after how last week felt. How have you been?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... I, um — I actually thought about not coming. Like seriously almost didn't. But I kept thinking about what you said, about it not being about punishment or whatever. So. Here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something I said stayed with you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Kind of, yeah. I mean it's still weird being here — I'm not, like, a therapy person. But I don't know. I've been more exhausted this week and I keep wondering if that's... related to things. Or whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me about the exhaustion. What does a night actually look like for you right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She doesn't sleep more than two hours at a stretch. My partner helps when he can but he has work, so it's mostly me. And by eight, nine o'clock I'm just... the wine is the only thing that makes the quiet feel okay. Like, I know how that sounds. But it's just — it takes the edge off. One glass, sometimes two. My doctor said a little is fine, so.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It gives you something to hold onto when the nights get really heavy.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Yeah. [pause] It's not like I'm getting drunk. I'm still — I'm aware. I'm still a functioning person. I just need something to, like, decompress after twelve hours of being someone's entire world.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And I'm curious about the other piece — the reason you're here. The court order. What comes up for you when you think about that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? It makes me angry. Sorry. But I made one mistake, one night, and now I'm sitting here like I'm some kind of — I don't know. My daughter was home with my partner, she was safe, it was one bad night. And it's like the whole system just... swooped in.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She was safe. You made sure of that. And you're sitting with how unfair this whole thing feels.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. [long pause] I mean, I get why the law is what it is, okay? I'm not stupid. But I don't have a problem problem. I'm just a really exhausted new mom who had one really bad night. That's different.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you imagine your daughter... a year from now, two years... what do you want for her? What kind of mom do you want to be in that picture?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want to be — [voice tightens] — I want to be actually there. Present, you know? Not just physically in the room but actually... seeing her. And I think sometimes — I wonder if the wine makes me less there. Like I'm in the room but I'm kind of dulled. [pause] She's four months old and she already looks at me like I'm everything and I don't always feel like I deserve that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: [long pause] She sees everything in you. And you're scared of not being able to hold all of that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I cry every day. I don't tell my partner because he already worries so much. But yeah. [pause] I know what it's like to have a mom who wasn't really there. And I swore — I swore I wasn't going to be that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me just try to hold all of this for a moment. There's a woman who found something that got her through the hardest nights — and she came back here today, because somewhere inside her she's asking whether that thing is getting between her and what she wants most. Being truly there for her daughter. The way no one was there for her.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...[exhales] Yeah. That's kind of exactly it. I don't want to stop coping, I just — maybe I want to cope differently? I don't even know what that looks like. But maybe. [quiet laugh] Maybe.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That 'maybe' — that is not nothing. You walked back in here today when you didn't have to feel like it. You named something real and true about your daughter just now. And you're sitting with something genuinely hard without running from it. That's not nothing at all.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: [small laugh, then quiet] I didn't think it would feel like this. I thought it'd be more like... being cross-examined. [pause] I think I can come back next week.

client_context: A 40-year-old single parent who has been drinking a bottle of wine nightly to cope with the stress of raising two kids alone. Knows it's too much but feels trapped.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you again. How are you doing after this past week?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Not great. I mean, it's fine, it's... I don't know. It was a rough week. I had that follow-up with my doctor and the results were... yeah. Not what I was hoping for.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds like a lot to carry — getting news like that when you're already stretched thin.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean, the doctor wasn't like, alarmed or anything, but she said the liver enzymes are still elevated and that I really need to — she used the word 'significantly' — reduce my drinking. And I just sat there nodding like I had it together but inside I was... I don't know. Spiraling, kind of.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So part of you was holding it together on the outside while something else entirely was happening inside. What was going through your mind in that moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? My first thought was — okay this is embarrassing — my first thought was, I cannot deal with this right now. Like, I have two kids who need dinner and homework help and Mia's got this big project due Friday and I'm supposed to what, just... stop? Like it's that easy? It's the only thing that makes the evenings survivable.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It helps you get through the evenings. And at the same time, you're sitting in a doctor's office hearing news that scared you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Yeah, it did scare me. I don't — I don't want to have liver problems. I'm forty years old, I'm the only parent these kids have. If something happens to me... God. I can't even go there.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You went there just now, even though it's painful. That says something about how seriously you're taking this.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I guess. I don't feel like I'm taking it seriously. I had a terrible week and I still drank every night. So.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're being really honest with yourself right now — which isn't easy. Can I ask, when you say the week was terrible, what was happening?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Marcus — my son, he's twelve — he got in trouble at school. Nothing huge, just, like, talking back to a teacher, but the school called me at work and I had to leave early and then my boss made this comment and I just... I came home and both kids were fighting and I thought, I just need five minutes. And the wine was there.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it's not just stress in the abstract — it's your job, your kids, everything hitting at once, and the wine became a way to get that five minutes of relief you desperately needed.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Yes. That's exactly it. And I know it's a crutch, I'm not stupid. But I don't have a partner to hand things off to, I don't have... I don't have a backup. So yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been holding up an enormous amount on your own for a long time. I want to reflect something back to you — you came in today after a hard week, you were honest about drinking every night, and you named what scares you. That's not what someone who doesn't care looks like.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I do care. I really do. I just — I feel so stuck. Like I can see the problem but I can't figure out how to fix it without the whole thing falling apart.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me see if I'm understanding where you are right now. The lab results shook you. You know the drinking is more than just a little stress relief at this point.
