And you're not looking for permission to keep going the way things are — you're trying to figure out if change is even possible given everything on your plate. Is that close?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. That's... yeah. I don't want to keep feeling like this. I don't. I just need to figure out how to get through a Tuesday night without it. Which sounds so small when I say it out loud but it feels... it feels impossible.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound small at all. It sounds like the exact right place to start. What would it mean for you — for your kids — if you found a way through a Tuesday night that didn't cost you anything the next morning?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: God. I'd feel... I think I'd feel like myself again? Like, the person I was before all this got so heavy. I want that. I actually want that.

client_context: A 34-year-old artist who believes alcohol fuels creativity. Has been drinking daily for years. Recently noticed the art has gotten worse, not better.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for joining me today, especially after everything you've been through this week. That took courage. So — tell me what's been going on from your perspective. What brought you to the ER?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... it was nothing, honestly. I hadn't eaten much and I had a few drinks and I just — I passed out. My roommate freaked out and called 911. It wasn't like, a big thing. I was fine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So in your mind, the circumstances lined up in a specific way — low food, alcohol — and your roommate's reaction felt like an overreaction to something you see as pretty explainable.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Like, yes. Thank you. Everyone's acting like I tried to... I don't know. I wasn't trying to hurt myself. I was just painting and lost track of time. That's what I do. I get in the zone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Painting is clearly central to who you are. What does a normal painting session look like for you — like, walk me through it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... I usually start in the late afternoon when the light is good. I'll pour a glass of wine, put on some music, and just... let go. The wine helps me stop overthinking. Without it I'm just staring at the canvas second-guessing every brushstroke. With it, I actually — I flow. It's been my process for like, ten years.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The wine quiets the inner critic. That makes sense — a lot of artists talk about needing to get out of their own heads. And you've built a whole ritual around it. I want to ask you something directly though, and I'm curious what you honestly think: how has the work been lately? The actual art.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
...

It's been... not great. I mean. I don't know. I look at stuff I made like five years ago and it has this — energy. This clarity. And now I finish something and I just feel... I don't even want to show it to anyone. I've been blaming the block on stress, or the market, or whatever, but...

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: But you're not fully buying that explanation anymore.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. No, I guess I'm not. I've been drinking more than a glass or two for a while now. And the sessions that were supposed to be freeing just feel... foggy. I wake up and I don't even remember finishing the piece. And then I look at it and it's — it's muddy. Everything's muddy.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That takes real honesty to say out loud. You came in defending something, and you're sitting here right now questioning whether that thing has actually been working against you. That's not easy.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I built my whole identity around this idea that I'm someone who drinks and makes art. Like, that's the story. The tortured artist, whatever. And if that's not true, then... what have I been doing? What have I been protecting?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What do you think you've been protecting?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Fear, probably. Like... what if I paint sober and it's still bad? Then I can't blame the block on anything. Then it's just — me. And maybe I'm not as good as I thought I was. The drinking gives me an excuse.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the alcohol hasn't just been fuel — it's also been a shield. And here's what I find striking: the artist who made that clear, energetic work five years ago? She existed before the drinking got heavier. That clarity you're missing — there's evidence it's already in you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: God. Yeah. I... yeah. I hadn't thought about it like that. It's like I've been borrowing against something and now I'm overdrawn.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a really sharp way to put it. Given everything you've just said — the muddy work, the fear, the shield, the ER visit — where does that leave you in terms of what you want to do next? What feels possible?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know if I'm ready to just stop cold. That terrifies me honestly. But... maybe I could try one session. Just one painting session, no wine, see what happens. Like, run the experiment. If it's a disaster, at least I know. But maybe — maybe it won't be.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I've heard today, because a lot happened in this conversation. You came in feeling like the ER was no big deal, and by the end you're describing a pattern you've privately noticed for a while — muddy work, lost sessions, a story about yourself you're not sure fits anymore. You're not ready to upend everything, and that's okay. But you came up with your own idea: one sober session. That's yours. And the fact that you can even imagine it — that tells me something about where you actually are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It tells you I'm scared but maybe not as stuck as I thought. ...Yeah. Okay. Maybe.

client_context: A 26-year-old software engineer with severe social anxiety who uses alcohol as liquid courage at every social event. Knows it's a crutch but terrified of life without it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's good to meet you. I know coming in today probably wasn't easy, especially if you've tried this before. I'd like to start by just hearing from you — in your own words, what's going on for you right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... yeah, hi. Sorry, I'm — I'm just a little nervous. I've done the therapy thing before and it kind of just... didn't go anywhere. My partner, Marcus, he basically said that he needed me to come. Like, it wasn't an ultimatum exactly, but it kind of was? He's worried about my drinking. So. Here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So there's pressure from Marcus, and at the same time you've been here before — done the work — and it didn't stick the way you hoped. That's a hard place to start from.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And I don't want you to think I'm, like, some kind of... I don't have a drinking problem in the way people picture it. I don't drink at home alone or whatever. It's just — I have really severe social anxiety, like clinically diagnosed, and alcohol just... turns it off. I can actually function at a party, talk to his coworkers, go to work events. Without it I just freeze up. So it's not nothing, it's actually useful.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It genuinely works. It gives you access to a version of yourself that can show up and get through those situations. What's it like, though — needing it in order to feel okay in those moments?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... I mean, it works, so I've always just kind of justified it. But last year I was at a coworker's birthday thing and I pre-gamed in the parking lot beforehand, like, alone in my car. And I remember sitting there thinking — this is embarrassing. Like, I'm twenty-six. I have a master's degree. And I cannot walk into a bar sober. That felt... that felt bad.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's real pain in that image — doing something that gets you through the moment but leaves you feeling ashamed of yourself afterward.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And Marcus... he's so patient, he really is, but I can see it wearing on him. Last month at his firm's dinner I had too much and I made this comment — it wasn't even that bad, objectively — but he just looked at me. And I knew. I knew I'd crossed something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What did you know, in that moment when he looked at you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That I was becoming someone... I don't know. Someone I didn't sign up to be. I went into software specifically because I could work from home most of the time, control my environment. I thought I could just manage it forever. But you can't. You can't opt out of every social thing. And the drinking keeps me from ever having to actually — like, deal with the anxiety. I just keep going around it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a genuinely clear-eyed thing to say about yourself — that you've built a whole workaround, and that the workaround is starting to cost you things that matter. That kind of self-awareness is not easy to sit with.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess. I just... I don't know what the alternative even looks like. Like, what do people do at parties? Just stand there being anxious? That sounds genuinely horrible. I've tried that. It's horrible.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you picture a life without alcohol as the solution, it just looks like... the same anxiety, but now with nothing to take the edge off. What would need to be different for that picture to not look so bleak?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... if the anxiety was actually treated, maybe? I tried medication once, it made me really foggy and I stopped after like six weeks. And the therapists I've seen — they were fine — but we just kind of talked about things in general. No one ever really went into the anxiety specifically. Like, directly. I don't know if that's a thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing, and you can tell me if I'm getting it right. The drinking has been a real solution to a real problem — anxiety that is serious and that nobody has actually helped you treat at the root. It's worked, but it's starting to cost you your relationship, your sense of yourself, moments you can't take back. You've tried other things before, but nothing has ever really targeted the anxiety directly. And somewhere in all of that, you're wondering if maybe — with the right support — things could actually be different.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. Yeah, that's — when you say it like that it's kind of a lot to take in. But yeah. That's pretty much it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I don't want to rush past that. Take a breath. If you let yourself imagine — even just as a thought experiment — what your life might look like if the anxiety had less of a hold on you. Not gone, just... less in charge. What changes?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I'd probably be better at my job. I avoid so many meetings, I let other people present things I built because standing up in front of people makes me feel physically sick. And with Marcus... we'd fight less. He's not really fighting about the drinking, I think. He's fighting because I go away when things get social, I just disappear into myself or into the bottle. I know that. I've always known that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just connected something really important — the anxiety, the drinking, and the life you actually want. And you named it clearly, without me prompting you. A lot of people sit in that chair for a long time before they can do that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've been thinking about it for a while. I just didn't want to say it out loud because... saying it out loud makes it real. But maybe — I don't know — maybe real is okay. I think I actually want to try this time. Not just because Marcus asked me to. Like, for me.

client_context: A 21-year-old college senior who binge drinks every weekend. Friends staged an intervention but the student sees it as normal college behavior.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's good to see you again. How have things been going since we last met?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... fine? I don't know, it's been kind of a weird week. My friends are still being weird about the whole thing, acting like I'm some kind of alcoholic or whatever. It's just, like, I don't know why everyone's making such a big deal out of it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the tension with your friends is still sitting with you. That sounds uncomfortable, carrying that into the week.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, uncomfortable is one word for it. More like... annoying? Like, I went out Thursday and Jake literally texted me the next morning asking how much I drank. My own friend. It feels like everyone's watching me now and it's — it's a lot. I didn't sign up for this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You didn't ask for all this scrutiny, and now it feels like every move you make is being monitored. That kind of pressure from people you trust... it makes sense that would feel like a lot.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. And look, Thursday wasn't even that bad. I had like six, maybe seven drinks over the whole night. That's nothing. Anyone at my school does that. I don't understand why I'm the one sitting in a counselor's office right now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It really doesn't feel fair — especially when from where you're standing, Thursday looks pretty normal. What was going on for you that night, before you headed out?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I had a brutal week. Two midterms, a group project that's a total disaster, and then the whole intervention thing still kind of... lingering. I just needed to shut my brain off, you know? I wasn't trying to get wrecked. I just wanted one normal night.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You were carrying a lot — academically, socially — and Thursday was your way of getting some relief from all of that. And even so, part of you is still thinking about why this keeps coming up.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. I guess. I don't know, sometimes I wonder if — like, it's always when things get hard, that's when I really want to drink. But that's just how people deal with stress, right? That's not a thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You noticed something real just now — that the drinking and the hard moments seem to line up. That took some honesty to say out loud.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, I'm not saying it's a problem. I'm just... I don't know. It's weird. My dad drank a lot when I was a kid and I swore I'd never be like that, and obviously I'm not, but sometimes I catch myself and I'm like — hm. Whatever, it's different.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's this thing you said — 'I swore I'd never be like that.' That sounds like it matters to you. A lot.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, obviously. My dad was... it wasn't great. He wasn't violent or anything but he was just, like, gone. Every night, just gone. I hated it. So yeah, that matters to me. But I'm not him. I still go to class, I have a 3.2, I have friends. It's totally different.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So being present — really present — is something you value deeply because of what it felt like when someone wasn't there for you. And you're working hard to be a different kind of person than that. What would it look like for you to feel really confident you're on that track?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know... I guess if the drinking felt like a choice instead of just, like, the automatic thing I do. Like, if I could take it or leave it. Right now it kind of feels like I don't really think about it, I just... do it. And maybe that's what's freaking me out a little.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a really important thing to notice — the difference between choosing something and just being on autopilot with it. You came in today frustrated, feeling watched and judged... and somewhere in this conversation you found that. That's yours. You did that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... I still think everyone's overreacting. But maybe — I don't know. Maybe I can at least think about what it would look like to be more intentional about it or whatever. I'm not making any promises.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: No promises needed. You came in today feeling like everyone was against you, and you're leaving with something you noticed for yourself — that you want drinking to feel like a real choice, not just a default. That's a different place than where we started. I'm glad you came in.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I guess I am too. ...A little.

client_context: A 39-year-old diagnosed with depression who self-medicates with alcohol. Has tried therapy before and dropped out. Skeptical but willing to give it one more try.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey Marcus, glad you got connected okay - telehealth can be a little unpredictable sometimes. I don't want to assume anything about what brought you here today, so I'd rather just hear it from you. What's on your mind as we get started?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... look, I'll be straight with you. I'm here because HR basically told me I had to be. That was the deal - come to this or start looking for a new job. I've done the therapy thing before and it was a complete waste of time, so I'm not exactly... I don't know. I'm not holding my breath here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you've been through this before, it didn't do much, and now you're back - this time because someone else decided you needed to be. That's a frustrating place to start.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. And the thing that really gets me is - I've been at that company eleven years. Eleven. And one bad day and suddenly I'm like, the guy with the problem. It got completely blown out of proportion. I don't even know why I'm defending myself to you, you don't know any of these people.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Eleven years - that's real loyalty. And it sounds like this felt like a betrayal of that. What actually happened that day, from where you were standing?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... okay, so I came in, I'd had a rough couple of nights. My manager pulls me into a meeting about some report, and the data was wrong before I even touched it. And I just... I lost it a little. Said some things. I don't even fully remember all of it, honestly. But it wasn't - people make mistakes. I wasn't violent or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You lost it a little... and you're also telling me you don't fully remember what was said. I'm not judging that - I'm just noticing those two things together. Sounds like it scared you a bit too.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. A little. My manager looked at me like I was someone else. And I hate that. I've always been the steady one on my team. That's not... that's not who I am. Or it wasn't, I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That gap - between who you know yourself to be and how you showed up that day - what do you make of that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... the depression's been bad lately. And when it gets bad, I drink more. And I know that's - I'm not stupid, I know that's not exactly the recommended approach. But it's the only thing that actually quiets it, you know? The noise in my head. At least for a few hours I'm not just... grinding through it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the drinking isn't just about drinking - it's been doing a job for you. Keeping the depression manageable enough to get through the day. And at the same time, it sounds like it might be the thing that's starting to cost you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's kind of exactly it. Which is the part that makes no sense to me - it helps and it doesn't help at the same time. And I've been in that loop for a while now and I don't... I honestly don't know how to get out of it. That's the part that scares me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Setting aside what HR wants, setting aside your manager - what do you actually want for yourself?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want to feel like myself again. Like the guy I was five, six years ago. I used to be good at my job. I went to the gym. I had a social life, actual friends. Now it's just - work, go home, drink enough to sleep, repeat. That's not... that's not a life, is it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just pull together what I've heard, because there's a lot here. You came in ready to write this off, and you had good reasons for that. But in the last little while you've told me you know something is wrong, that the pattern you're in is costing you, and that there's a version of yourself you want to get back to. That person - the one who was good at his job, went to the gym, had a life - you can still describe him in real detail. He hasn't disappeared.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
...

Yeah. Yeah, he is still in there somewhere. I just - I don't know if I can find my way back. I've felt stuck for so long it's hard to even imagine things being different. But I don't know, talking to you right now... it doesn't feel as pointless as I thought it was going to.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You walked in here ready to go through the motions - and instead you've been more honest in the last half hour than you maybe planned to be. That's not a small thing. What do you think made that possible?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I'm just tired. Tired of feeling like this and pretending it's fine. And maybe I needed someone who wasn't going to freak out or hand me a pamphlet. You just kind of - you listened. My last therapist had a worksheet ready like two minutes in. That's not... I can't do that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: No worksheets. And I want you to know - everything you brought in here today, the depression, the drinking, the skepticism about all of this - none of it changes anything for me. We can work with all of it. So before we wrap up: what would one thing look like, just one, that you'd want to be different a month from now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I just want to wake up and not immediately dread the day. That's it. That's the whole thing. One morning where I don't feel like I'm already behind before I've gotten out of bed. That would... that would mean everything to me.

client_context: A 55-year-old who lost their spouse 8 months ago and has been drinking to numb the pain. Isolated from friends and family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm really glad you came in today. I know it can take a lot just to walk through a door like this, especially the first time... Can you tell me a little bit about what brought you here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? My boyfriend. He gave me kind of an ultimatum — said he'd leave if I didn't get some kind of help. So. Here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came even though it wasn't really your own idea. That tells me something — maybe there's a part of you that's at least willing to see what this is about.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I've done this before — the whole counseling thing — and it didn't... I mean, my husband passed away eight months ago, and I just... I drink sometimes. To sleep. That's all. It's not like I'm falling down drunk every night or anything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like the drinking has become a way to get through — especially since losing your husband. What's it been like, these past eight months?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... dark. I don't know how else to say it. I used to have this whole life, and now I just... I wake up and the house is so quiet, and I pour a glass of wine and it takes the edge off for a little while. I know you're going to tell me that's a problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm not here to tell you anything. It sounds like that glass of wine gives you a few hours of quiet in a life that feels very, very heavy.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well. The other counselors said that too — that they understood, that they weren't judging me — and then we'd do the exercises and the worksheets and... nothing changed. I'd go home and Gerald still wasn't there. He's still not there. What is any of this supposed to do about that?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Nothing can bring Gerald back. And I think you already know that — and that's the hardest part of all of this. You've tried before, and the pain was still waiting when you got home. Of course you're wondering why this would be any different.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I just... I'm so tired. I'm tired of being sad, and I'm tired of pretending I'm okay, and I'm tired of feeling like a stranger in my own life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A stranger in your own life... can you say more about that? Who were you, before all of this?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I had friends. We had a garden — Gerald and I — and I used to host big dinners, I was the one people called when things were hard. And now I haven't... God, I haven't even called my sister in three months. I don't know why. I just can't face it. Any of it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The woman who kept the garden, who hosted those dinners, who everyone called when things were hard — she's still in there. She's been through something devastating, but I can actually hear her right now, in the way you're talking.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... hm. I don't know. Maybe. I used to think of myself as a pretty strong person. I always handled things, I was the one who held it together. And now I can't even answer the phone when my sister calls.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me see if I'm getting this right. You came in today, not really for yourself, but something in you showed up anyway. You've been carrying eight months of grief almost completely alone, in a house that's gotten very quiet. You've felt like a stranger to yourself — like the capable, connected woman you were has somehow gone somewhere else. And underneath all of it, there's a part of you that actually misses her. That woman with the garden.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you put it like that... yeah. Yeah, I do miss her. I miss being me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's something real to hold onto. If you were going to take just one small step — nothing dramatic, just one tiny thing — back toward that version of yourself, what might it be?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... I don't know. Maybe I'd call my sister. Or just... go outside. Gerald and I had a morning walk we used to do, same route every day, and I haven't... maybe I could do that again. By myself. I think about it sometimes.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's not a small thing. Imagining yourself on that walk again — without him — and being willing to even consider it. You walked in here today not sure what for. And now you're talking about morning walks.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know if I'll actually do it. But... I think about it. And maybe that's something. Yeah. Maybe.

client_context: A 38-year-old mandated by court to attend counseling after a second DUI. Furious about being forced to be here. Sees the system as unfair.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came back. I know last week ended rough — what's it been like since we talked?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: What do you think it's been like? I got slapped with another violation notice for missing a check-in. Because of paperwork. Paperwork. And now I gotta sit here and — you know what, forget it. This whole thing is a joke. I didn't ask to be here, my buddy called the judge, the judge made this mandatory, and here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're furious. Feels like no matter what you do, the system finds another way to jam you up.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly. And now I gotta come in here and — what, tell you my feelings? I'm 38 years old. I had a few drinks, that's it. My buddy calls it an 'intervention,' the judge calls it a 'pattern.' It's not a pattern. I had a bad month. A bad couple months. That doesn't make me... whatever they're trying to call me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me about this past week. You said you had a setback — what actually happened?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I went out Friday. Just a bar, couple guys from work. I wasn't — I didn't even plan on drinking, actually, which is the stupid part. I had soda at first. And then... um... something came up with my daughter earlier that day and I just — it was easier to not think about it, you know? So I had a few. And then more than a few.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something with your daughter hit you hard, and the drinking put some distance between you and that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She... she told my ex she doesn't want me at her recital. She's nine. Nine years old and she doesn't want her dad there. And I know — I know why. I'm not an idiot. But I didn't wanna sit with that all night, I just... yeah. I drank.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does it cost you — not the legal stuff, not the court, but what does the drinking actually cost you with her?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Everything. Probably... I don't know, maybe everything. Her mom keeps sending me these texts like, 'This is what you're doing to her.' And I want to fire back, say it's not fair, but... when I missed her birthday last year because I got arrested, that wasn't the judge's fault. That was me. I can't — I can't spin that one.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took something to say. You don't strike me as someone who admits that kind of thing easily.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm not — look, I don't think I'm perfect, okay? I know I've screwed some things up. I just hate being treated like I'm some... textbook alcoholic or whatever. I grew up watching real drunks. My dad was — my dad was bad. Like, bad bad. I'm not him. I show up. Mostly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're not your father. I believe that. So what does 'not being him' actually look like — with her, specifically?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It looks like... showing up. Not disappearing the way he did. She still texts me sometimes — just not the big things anymore. She used to tell me stuff. Now it's like one-word replies. But she still reaches out, so... I think she wants me around. She just doesn't trust that I'll stay.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She hasn't written you off. And some part of you is holding onto that — like it's the thing that still matters most.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I... I don't know how to do any of this without — when things get heavy, the bottle is just there. It's always been there. I get that that's the problem, I'm not stupid. I just don't — I don't know what I'm supposed to do instead. That's the part nobody tells you.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me say back what I'm hearing — you walked in here angry today, and that anger is real. But underneath it there's a man who is scared of losing his daughter the same way he lost his own father. Who drank last Friday not because it felt good, but because sitting with that pain alone was too much. And who, somewhere underneath all of it, is asking whether things could actually be different.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you put it like that... I mean. Yeah. That's... I hate how much that's right. I thought I was just pissed off this whole time. But I've been scared, haven't I. Like — the whole time.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Not for the judge, not for your ex — what would it need to look like for you to walk into that next recital?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She'd have to trust me first. And I can't build that by falling apart every time something hurts. I don't know if I can flip a switch, like I'm not gonna pretend it's that simple. But... I want to get there. I want to be the kind of dad she can actually count on. That's — that's what I want. That's mine, not the court's.

client_context: A 72-year-old with chronic pain who has been mixing alcohol with pain medication. Family is terrified. Doesn't want to burden anyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm really glad you came in today, Dorothy. There's no agenda here, no pressure. We can just... take our time. I wonder if you could start by telling me, in your own words, what brought you in.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Harold made me come. My husband. He's been going on and on for weeks now, and I just — I figured if I came once, he'd settle down and stop looking at me like I'm some kind of... anyway. I don't really see what the big fuss is about, honestly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Harold's been worried, and you came today partly to... put his mind at ease a little.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's about the size of it. I'm seventy-two years old. I raised three children, I buried a sister, I managed this household for forty-six years. And now suddenly everybody has opinions about what I do in my own home. It's — it's a bit much.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've carried a tremendous amount over the years. ...What's day-to-day life been like for you lately, Dorothy? At home, I mean.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's not easy. My back, and both hips now. The doctor keeps adjusting things but nothing really — it never fully takes it away. You just push through. That's what you do at my age. You don't complain, you push through. The wine in the evening, it just takes the edge off. That's all it is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You push through. Even when the pain is still there, underneath everything, all day long.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well what's the alternative? I'm not going to just lie in bed. I cook, I help when the grandchildren visit, I manage. It's... the evenings get hard. The tightness won't let up and the pills only do so much and I just — I want one hour. One quiet hour. Is that really so terrible?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That one quiet hour sounds like it means something really important to you. I'm curious — what does it feel like, when the wine starts to work and that tightness finally lets up a little?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Relief. Just relief. My shoulders drop. I can sit in the chair without counting the seconds till I can shift positions again. I'm not out at a bar somewhere. I'm in my own living room. I didn't think it was — I didn't think anyone was getting hurt.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That relief sounds... enormous. After a whole day of pushing through, of managing everything quietly on your own, that moment in the evening is something you really hold onto.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yes. That's — yes, that's exactly it. I just want to not be thinking for a little while. About the pain, or what needs doing, or whether I'm being a bother to anyone. I didn't realize how much I was... waiting for it. Until Harold pointed that out and I got so angry at him. But then I thought about it later and I thought, well. Hm.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been carrying so much, for so long. And so quietly. Because you don't want to be a burden — that matters deeply to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I never wanted Harold worrying about me on top of everything else he's got. And the kids — they have their own lives, their own problems. I didn't want them looking at me like I'm something that needs fixing. But he cried last week. Harold. I haven't seen that man cry in forty years. And he said he was scared. He said he was scared of losing me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something shifted when you saw Harold cry. You've spent so much energy keeping things quiet, not being a burden... and then that moment cracked something open.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I keep seeing his face. And I thought — I've been so focused on just getting through each day that I didn't notice what it was doing to him. Or maybe to me. My doctor did say, the mixing — the wine and the pain medication — he said that wasn't safe. I just sort of... nodded. And then didn't really let it in, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Part of you did hear it, though. And I think that part of you is sitting here with me right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Maybe. I don't want to be the kind of woman who can't — who loses control of herself. But I'm honestly not sure anymore where the pain ends and the habit begins. That frightens me a little, if I'm being truthful. I don't say that to people. I don't usually say that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took real courage to say, Dorothy. And the fact that you're asking that question — that's not someone who's lost. That's someone with a great deal of strength still in her. ...What would it mean to you, do you think, if things could look a little different?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I suppose I'd like Harold to stop being scared. And I'd like — maybe there's something else for the pain, something I haven't tried. Someone with a bit more time to actually talk about it. I'm not promising anything, mind you. But I... I came today, didn't I. That's something.

client_context: A 29-year-old who moved to a new country alone and started drinking to cope with loneliness and cultural adjustment. Has no local support system.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Come on in, take a seat wherever you're comfortable. I'm Dr. Chen — most people just call me Sarah. There's no set agenda here, no paperwork you have to fill out first. I just want to understand a little about what brought you in today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My academic advisor basically told me I had to come. I didn't — look, I'm not here because I think I have some big issue. She overreacted. I had one bad morning and now I'm sitting here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So this wasn't really your idea. What did she see that made her think coming here would be worth your time?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She — okay, I came to class and I smelled like alcohol. From the night before. That's it. One time. And now apparently I need counseling. Where I'm from, people drink. Adults drink. It's not this huge scandal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: From your perspective, she turned one incident into something much bigger than it is.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. I'm twenty-nine years old. I've been managing my own life for a long time. I moved to a different country by myself — by myself — and no one batted an eye at that. But I have a few drinks and suddenly everyone's very concerned about me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Moving to a new country alone — that's not a small thing. What's that actually been like, day to day?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's fine. It's fine. I knew it would be an adjustment. I'm not naive. I just... everyone here already has their whole life figured out. Their friends, their families nearby, their routines. And you show up and you're just... nobody. You're invisible. And people are polite but it's not — it's not real.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Invisible. That's a specific kind of painful — being surrounded by people and still feeling like you're not really there.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I haven't said that out loud before. There's no one to say it to — that's the whole problem. Back home I had my mother, my cousins, my best friend. We'd talk every single day. Here I come home to... silence. So yeah, I pour a glass of wine. Sometimes the bottle. It helps. And I don't think that's a crime.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you're sitting in that silence — what does it actually feel like in your body, in your chest?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Like... like I made a mistake. Like I gave up everything and for what. And then I feel stupid for thinking that because of course it wasn't a mistake, I worked so hard to get here. But at night that voice gets loud. The drinking quiets it down. That's all it is. It's temporary.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You left behind everyone who knew you, you're carrying your studies, managing everything alone, and you're still questioning yourself for struggling. That takes a particular kind of strength just to keep going. And I'm also hearing — this doubt, this wondering if it was worth it — that's not stupidity. That's grief.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Grief. I... yeah. I didn't think of it that way. I keep telling myself to stop being dramatic. But I do miss — I miss my life. I miss feeling like I was a person who mattered to people around me. Not just a student ID number.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If things were even a little better here — not perfect, just better — what would that look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Someone to have coffee with. Someone who gets it — what it's like to be far from home and pretend you're okay all the time. I went to this cultural association at the university once, a few months ago. I didn't go back. I felt weird going alone. But it was... it was nice to hear people speaking my language. I forgot how much I missed that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something opened up for you in that room, even just for a little while. What got in the way of going back?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. Fear maybe. What if I try and it still doesn't — what if I'm still invisible even there. It's easier to not try than to try and still feel alone. But... I don't know. Maybe that's not a great reason to stay home with a bottle of wine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me pull together what I've heard from you today. You came here under pressure, you weren't sure this was worth your time — and then you told me something you haven't told anyone. You moved here alone and you found a silence waiting for you that you weren't prepared for. The drinking has been a way to get through the nights when that silence gets too loud. At the same time, there's a part of you that already knows what you're looking for — real connection, being known — and you even found a small door to that once and stepped back from it out of fear. That's not a character flaw. That's a very human way to protect yourself. But I hear you noticing that the protection might be costing you something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I think... I think I've been so focused on surviving here that I haven't tried to actually live here. Those aren't the same thing. And the drinking — I'm not going to say it's not a thing anymore. Maybe it's become more of a thing than I've wanted to admit. I'm not sure what I do with that yet. But... I'm glad I came in today. I didn't expect to say that.

client_context: A 36-year-old veteran who started heavy drinking after deployment. Views drinking as normal military culture. Wife threatened divorce.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey Marcus, good to have you on today. I appreciate you making the time — I know getting on a video call with a stranger isn't exactly how most guys want to spend a Wednesday afternoon. I wanted to start by just... hearing from you. What's going on from your perspective?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... my doctor basically made me do this. My labs came back weird and she said I had to talk to someone. I don't — look, I've been drinking since I was nineteen. Everyone in my unit drank. It's not like I have some big problem or whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So this feels more like something that was handed to you than something you chose to do.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. I'm not some... I don't sit around in a ditch somewhere. I work, I show up, I take care of my family. A few beers at night is just — that's how I decompress. That's what we did downrange and it's what I do now. I don't see why that's suddenly a crisis.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What was it like downrange — the drinking, the culture around it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's just... it's what you do. Long days, you come back, someone's got a handle of something and you sit around and just — you don't even have to talk about anything. It's just quiet. You know what I mean? Nobody's asking you anything. Nobody needs something from you for like an hour. That was... that was good.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That quiet sounds like it was really important. Just being with people and not having to explain yourself or perform for anyone.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it was. And I still — I guess I still need that. At home it's always something. The kids, the bills, Sarah's on me about... I don't know, everything. I just need to shut it off sometimes. Is that really so bad?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you say Sarah's on you — what does things look like at home right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She said... she said if I don't get it together she's taking the kids and leaving. And I just — I don't know, man. I don't know what she wants from me. I can't be whatever she's picturing in her head. I'm just trying to get through the day. I don't even know what getting it together means.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Getting through the day. Like that's the goal right now — not thriving, not fixing anything, just... surviving until it's over.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. That's it. I haven't — huh. I haven't thought about it like that but yeah. Just surviving. That's been the goal for like three years now and I didn't even realize it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You mentioned the kids. What are they like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: They're good. They're great, actually. My son's seven — he's obsessed with dinosaurs right now, like knows every single name, corrects me when I get them wrong. My daughter's four. She... she still runs to the door when she hears my truck pull up. Every single time.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She still runs to the door. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It matters. It matters a lot. I just... I worry sometimes that one day she won't. That she'll — I don't know. That she'll figure out that I'm not who she thinks I am. Like she's got this picture of her dad and I'm scared she's gonna see through it eventually.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it mean to you to still be the guy she runs to — five, ten years from now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's... I mean, that's everything. That's — I want to be there. I want to actually be there, not just in the house. Because I'm in the house but I'm not... I've been checked out and I know that. I know that. Maybe that's — maybe that's the thing I should actually be worried about, not just my liver numbers.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me make sure I'm hearing you right. You came in today because your doctor pushed you to, and you weren't sure any of this applied to you. But as we've been talking, you've shared that things at home are really strained — Sarah's at a breaking point — and underneath that there's this real fear that you're losing connection with your kids. The drinking has been your way to get that quiet you needed, going all the way back to deployment. And now you're starting to wonder if it might be getting in the way of the thing you actually care most about — being present, being the dad she runs to. That's what I'm hearing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Yeah, that — that's right. I didn't think I was gonna say any of that today. I came in here thinking I'd just wait for you to call me an alcoholic and then I was gonna leave. But... I don't know. Maybe I should actually think about some of this stuff.

client_context: A 42-year-old construction worker who drinks a six-pack every night. Referred by his doctor after abnormal liver tests. Thinks the doctor is overreacting.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, thanks for joining me today. I know telehealth can feel a little weird at first — sitting in your own living room talking to a screen. How are you doing?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, I'm fine. I guess. My wife set this whole thing up — she's the one who wanted me to do this. The doctor says my liver numbers are off or whatever, and suddenly everyone's acting like I'm dying.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it sounds like this wasn't exactly your idea, coming here today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. Look, I respect doctors, I do. But I've been doing the same thing for twenty years and I'm fine. I work construction, okay? It's a hard job. You come home, you have a few beers, you decompress. That's just... that's just what you do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Twenty years of hard physical work. That's no small thing. Your body takes a beating on a job site — I get why winding down matters at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Nobody ever talks about that side of it. It's not like I'm sitting at a desk. I'm lifting, I'm moving, I'm out in the heat. My back's shot, my knees hurt. A six-pack is... it takes the edge off. It's not like I'm some kind of alcoholic.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're not here because of a label. I'm not interested in putting a word on you. What I'm curious about is — you mentioned the liver results. What did the doctor actually say to you, in that appointment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: He said my... ALT or AST, one of those things, was elevated. And he asked how much I drink and I told him, and he got this look on his face like... I don't know. He said if I keep going the way I'm going there could be damage. Serious damage, he said. But doctors always say stuff like that to scare you.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And yet you're here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Yeah, I guess I am. I mean, my wife was freaking out. And my buddy — we worked together for fifteen years — he died two years ago. Liver failure. He was... he was a drinker. More than me, but. I don't know. It's not the same.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a real loss. I'm sorry about your friend. And it sounds like part of you made a connection there, even if another part of you is pushing that away.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. I don't like to think about it. He was only 48. And he looked bad at the end, like real bad. But he was drinking way more than me. Like, I'm talking a bottle of vodka a day kind of thing. That's different.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're right that there are differences. And I also hear that you're aware the line exists somewhere — you're thinking about where you are relative to that line. What would it mean for you if the doctor is right, even a little?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I got a daughter. She's nine. And my wife... she puts up with a lot. I'm not, I'm not saying I'm a bad guy, I'm a good dad, but I know some nights I'm not... totally present, you know? Like I'm there but I'm not there. And I — look, I don't want to be sick. I don't want my kid to see me sick.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Being present for your daughter — that matters to you. That's clear. And you've got enough self-awareness to notice when the drinking gets in the way of that. That takes honesty, and not everyone gets there.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I love that kid more than anything. She asked me last month why I smell like beer all the time. Nine years old. That... that hit me different. I kind of just brushed it off but it stuck with me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing — tell me if I'm getting this right. You came in today partly because your wife pushed you, but also because something in you responded to those lab results. You've lost a friend to liver disease, and it scared you more than you want to admit. And now your daughter's asking questions. You're not ready to call it a problem, but you're also not as sure as you were an hour ago that everything's fine.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... yeah, that's — that's pretty much it. I don't want to blow this out of proportion. But I also don't want to be stupid about it, you know? Like, maybe I could cut back a little. See what happens. I'm not saying I have a problem, but... maybe I could try.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That openness — even just being willing to try — that's actually a big deal. You walked in here ready to argue with me, and instead you're talking about your daughter, your health, what you want your life to look like. What would cutting back even look like for you, in a realistic way?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know, like... maybe not every night? Or like, two or three instead of six? I'd have to find something else to do with my hands. Watch TV, I don't know. It sounds stupid when I say it out loud but... I think I could try that. I'm not promising anything. But I could try.

client_context: A 65-year-old retiree who started drinking more since retirement due to loneliness and loss of purpose. Doctor flagged liver concerns at last checkup.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thank you for coming in today. I know this is the first time you've done something like this, and that takes real courage. There's no agenda here — no right or wrong thing to say. I just want to understand what's going on for you. What brought you in?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well... the doctor said some of my liver numbers were off. So. Here I am. [pause] I'm not really sure what I'm supposed to say. I've never done this kind of thing before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Here you are. [pause] It sounds like those results gave you a real jolt.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I guess they did. I've been... it's been a strange few years, since I retired. I thought I'd enjoy it, you know? Travel, relax. But it's just been... quiet. Too quiet. My wife passed three years ago and, uh... I don't know. I started having a drink in the evenings to sort of take the edge off. And then it became two. And then I don't really know when it became more than that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You lost your wife. And then retirement came, and with it this... silence. And somewhere in that, drinking became a way to get through the evenings. [long pause] That's a tremendous amount of loss happening all at once.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I suppose. I never really put it together like that. I always just thought I was being... weak. My father would've said toughen up, you know? [quiet] But some nights it's — it's genuinely the only thing that helps me sleep. The house is so damn empty.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's the only thing that helps you sleep in that empty house. [pause] And at the same time... you got those lab results. And you came here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [long pause] I'm 65. If I wreck my liver now... I mean... [trails off] What's the point anyway. [catches himself] That's a terrible thing to say, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound terrible to me. It sounds honest. [pause] What did you mean — what's the point?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. I wake up most mornings and I think... okay, so what now. You know? At least when Margaret was alive there was someone who needed me to function. To show up. Now I just rattle around that house. [voice cracks slightly] I haven't had dinner with another person in... God. Six weeks, maybe more.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Six weeks. [long pause] You've been carrying all of this completely alone. Every night, in that quiet.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [pause] You know, it's strange. Hearing myself say it out loud like that. I've been trying to pretend this is just... normal. This is just what it looks like to get old. But maybe it's not. Maybe I've just been — I don't know — going through the motions. Waiting for something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something in you isn't convinced this is just how it has to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I still go out to the garden every morning. Rain or shine. Even when I feel terrible, even when I've had too much the night before. [small, quiet laugh] Margaret used to say I loved those tomatoes more than I loved her. [pause] I don't know. I think... I think I still want things. I'm just not sure how to get there anymore.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Every single morning, you get up and you tend to that garden. Even the hard mornings. [pause] That's not nothing. That tells me a great deal about who you are — there's still something in you that wants to grow things. That wants to show up.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I never thought of it that way. [pause] My son — he's been asking me to come visit. I keep saying no. Making excuses. I think I've just been... hiding. From him. From everyone. I'm ashamed, I think. That this is what I've become.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in here today. That's you choosing not to hide, at least for this hour. [pause] And what I hear underneath the shame is a man who misses his son. Who misses being needed. Who still gets up every morning even when there's no reason to.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [long pause, exhales] Yeah. I do miss him. I miss a lot of things. But maybe — I don't know — maybe some of them I can still have. Maybe it's not too late for all of it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to reflect back what I've heard today, if that's okay. You came in because your body sent you a warning. You've been carrying enormous grief — losing Margaret, losing your sense of purpose, losing the structure that told you who you were. Drinking crept in quietly to fill that void, to get you through the nights. And yet — you tend that garden every morning. You still feel the pull toward your son. And sitting here today, something shifted a little. It sounds to me like there's still a lot of living you want to do.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [quiet, long pause] Yeah, there is. I'd really like to figure out how to get there. I think — I think maybe the first thing I do when I get home is call my son. I've been putting it off for months. That's where I'll start.

client_context: A 34-year-old artist who believes alcohol fuels creativity. Has been drinking daily for years. Recently noticed the art has gotten worse, not better.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm really glad you came back today. Last week felt like a lot to process, and showing up again — that says something about you. How have things been since we last spoke?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... okay, I guess. I mean, I almost didn't come. My sister drove me again, so... yeah. I kept thinking like, what's the point, you know? I don't really know why I'm here, honestly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What was going through your mind when you were deciding whether to come back?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know... I'm not — I don't think I have a drinking problem, that's the thing. It's just how I work. It's always been how I work. But then I looked at some pieces I did last month and something felt... off. And I couldn't stop thinking about that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something felt off when you looked at your recent work.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Like, they're technically fine — maybe even technically better in some ways — but they're... hollow. There's nothing in them. And I can't tell if that's the drinking or if I'm just losing it as an artist, which is honestly the scarier possibility.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Losing your identity as an artist — that's a real and painful fear. I'm curious, when did you first start to believe that drinking and your creativity were connected?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... forever? In art school everyone drank. The best people drank. There was this whole mythology — like you had to suffer and drink and stay up all night to make anything real. And my thesis work, the stuff that actually got me noticed... I did most of that drunk at 2am. So it just kind of became fact.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the belief got built up over time, anchored to a real moment that mattered deeply — your thesis work — and reinforced by a whole community sharing the same story. It became woven into who you are as an artist.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. And now I'm... what, supposed to just dismantle that? Like... what if I take the drinking away and there's nothing there? What if the work was never really mine — it was just the alcohol? ... That's the thought I can't get rid of.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's one of the most painful fears I hear from artists — and it deserves to be taken seriously, not dismissed. Would it be okay if I shared what we actually know about alcohol and creative work?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. Sure.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Alcohol can produce a genuine feeling — looseness, disinhibition, a sense of flow — that people experience as creative inspiration. That feeling is real. But when we look at the actual output over time, alcohol consistently degrades complex creative thinking. The feeling of being inspired and the quality of the work start to pull apart from each other. What you noticed in those pieces — that hollow quality — that's not you losing your talent. That may be exactly what alcohol does, on a long enough timeline.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: So the feeling is real but... the work isn't keeping up with it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Exactly. And you noticed that divergence yourself — before I said anything. What does it mean to you that you caught that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess... it means I still care. About the work. Like some part of me hasn't completely checked out. I've been telling myself this story for so long — that this is just who I am — and maybe it isn't. Or maybe it doesn't have to be.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came back when part of you wanted to stay away. You looked at your work honestly and didn't flinch from what you saw. And now you're questioning a story you've carried for over a decade. That's a lot of hard honesty in a short amount of time. Given all of that — what feels even a little bit possible to you right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... maybe trying to paint sober. Just once. To see. I'm terrified of it, honestly. But I'm more terrified of that hollow feeling becoming permanent. Like — what if there's something there without it? I've never actually tested that. Not as an adult.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a significant shift — from 'this is just how I work' to 'I've never actually tested that.' You're not throwing out your whole identity. You're just asking an honest question. And it sounds like it's coming from you — from what you care about — not from your sister, not from me.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. It is mine. I mean, I'm still scared. But... it feels different from last week. Like I'm finally asking the question for myself.

client_context: A 40-year-old single parent who has been drinking a bottle of wine nightly to cope with the stress of raising two kids alone. Knows it's too much but feels trapped.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know it's not always easy to walk through a door like this one. Before we get into anything formal, I just want to know — what was it like for you, making this appointment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I almost didn't come. I've done this before — the whole counseling thing — and it never really... I don't know. It never sticks. But my doctor basically scared the hell out of me with these lab results so. Here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something your doctor said was alarming enough that you pushed through all that doubt and showed up anyway. That took something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I have kids. Two kids. I can't just — I don't have the luxury of falling apart. So yeah, when she said my liver enzymes were elevated, I thought, okay. Fine. I'll go talk to someone again.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your kids are a huge part of this for you. I hear that. Can you tell me a little more about what a typical day looks like — like, what you're carrying?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's just... everything. I wake up, I get them to school, I go to work, I come home, I make dinner, I help with homework, I do laundry, I do it all — alone. There's no one else. And by like nine or ten at night when they're finally asleep, I just... I need something to just turn my brain off. Is that so terrible?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're exhausted. Completely, bone-deep exhausted. And the wine at the end of the night — it gives you the only quiet you get all day.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Yeah, that's — that's exactly it. It's like, the whole day I'm holding everything together and then finally, finally I can just... exhale. And I know a bottle is too much, okay? I know that. I'm not an idiot.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You already know. You've known for a while, sounds like.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I do. But knowing doesn't — like, what am I supposed to do instead? Meditate? I don't have time to meditate. I barely have time to pee alone. And the last counselor I saw just kept giving me worksheets. Like, here's a coping skills worksheet. Thanks, super helpful.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been handed solutions that didn't fit your actual life. That's — I can understand why you'd walk in here skeptical. I'd be skeptical too.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just don't want to be lectured. I get enough of that from my mother. I know what I'm doing isn't great. I don't need someone to tell me wine is bad for me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm not here to lecture you. I mean that. What I'm actually curious about — and you don't have to have a clean answer — is what scares you most when you imagine this continuing another year. Another five years.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
...

My daughter is twelve. She notices things. She... last month she asked me why there were so many bottles in the recycling bin. And I made up some excuse, I don't even remember what I said, but she looked at me like... like she already knew I was lying. And that — god, that killed me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She saw you. And you saw her seeing you. And that moment has stayed with you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't want her to grow up thinking that's just... what you do when life gets hard. I don't want that to be what she learns from me. I worked so hard to give them something better than what I had, and here I am doing the same thing my dad did, just — wine instead of whiskey. Same thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So there's this version of yourself — the mother you want to be for her — and you can see her clearly. And there's also the woman who is utterly depleted by nine PM and needs relief. Both of those are real. Both make complete sense. I'm wondering what it would mean to you if you could actually find some ground between those two things.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I think it would mean I actually have a shot at this. Like, not just white-knuckling it for a week and then falling apart again. Something that actually — I don't know — lasts. Maybe. I haven't let myself think about it like that in a while.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You haven't let yourself hope about it. Until just now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Maybe. Yeah. Maybe just now.

client_context: A 32-year-old ER nurse who started drinking heavily during the pandemic. Feels guilty but says it's the only way to decompress after traumatic shifts.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know walk-in appointments can feel a little... unexpected. Before anything else, I want to be upfront with you — nothing you share here gets reported back to your employer unless you're in immediate danger. So, with that said, what's on your mind coming in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... HR said I had to be here, so. [pause] I'm not really sure what this is supposed to accomplish. I don't — I don't have like, a drinking problem or whatever. I just had a really rough night and I made a mistake at work. One mistake. In eight years.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So this feels like something that was imposed on you, not something you walked in here choosing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Yeah. Eight years, not a single incident on my record. And now because of one thing they've got me sitting in a... [gestures around] I'm sorry. I'm not trying to be rude. I'm just — I'm frustrated. It feels like I'm being treated like I'm some kind of liability.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Eight years is a long time. And it sounds like that record matters a lot to you — your identity as a nurse is wrapped up in it. I'm wondering, and you don't have to have a neat answer for this — what do you think changed?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: The pandemic. I mean... what do you think? [quieter] I held phones up to people's faces so they could say goodbye to their families. Over and over. And then you go home. And you're supposed to just... sleep? The drinking started because it was the only thing that actually turned my brain off. Like, nothing else worked. Not exercise, not whatever, not meditation apps. [pause] So.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It became your off switch.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [pause] Yeah, that's... that's actually exactly what it is. And I know how that sounds — I'm a nurse. I know what alcohol does, I've seen cirrhosis, I know. But after a shift where you coded three people and only one made it back... a glass of wine stopped cutting it a long time ago. I needed to actually stop feeling things for a few hours.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been carrying a weight that most people genuinely can't imagine. And the drinking has been how you've survived it, night after night. I want to ask you about the incident at work — when that moment happened, when you caught yourself, what was going through your head?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I was... I couldn't think straight. Not like tired-tired, like — my brain wasn't tracking. And I caught it, I caught the med error before anything happened to the patient. But in that second I just... I knew. I knew I wasn't okay. [voice wavers] I've never felt like that at work before. Not once. That scared me more than anything HR said afterward.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Even in that moment — foggy, exhausted, scared — you caught it. The part of you that became a nurse to protect people was still there, still working. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know if I deserve credit for that, I — [exhales] But yeah. It scared me because nursing is the only thing I've ever actually wanted to do. Like, since I was a kid. If I lose that... [trails off] I can't lose that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing, and tell me if I'm getting it wrong. You went through something genuinely traumatic during the pandemic — things that would knock anyone sideways. Drinking became a way to survive those nights, to function. And now there's a part of you that's frightened, because you're starting to see it bleeding into the one thing that defines you — your patients, your work, who you are when you put that badge on.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you say it like that... yeah. [long pause] Yeah, that's it. I think I've been telling myself it's fine, it's under control, because I couldn't let myself look at it directly. But it's... it's affecting my work now. I know that. I think I've known that for a while and just kept not dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it look like for you to get that version of yourself back — the one who goes home after a hard shift and can actually rest?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: God. [soft, surprised laugh] I haven't let myself think about that in... I don't even know how long. I think it would mean waking up and not already feeling behind. Being actually present with my patients, not just going through the motions. Maybe not dreading going in. [quieter] I used to love going in.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That person — the one who loved going in — she's still in there. What you're describing isn't who you've become, it's what happened to you. And you're still fighting for your patients even now. That's who you are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... yeah. [quietly] I think I needed to hear that. I don't know where to start, but I — I want to figure this out. For real. Not because HR sent me here. Because I don't want to lose myself in this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in today not knowing what to expect, maybe thinking this was just a box to check. And somewhere in this hour, something shifted — you named what this has been costing you, and what you want back. That takes real honesty. So, thinking about what's actually realistic for you right now — what feels like a possible first step, even a small one?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... coming back. Regularly, not just once. I don't think one conversation is going to fix eight years of — whatever this is. And maybe looking into whether there's like, a program or something structured. I don't want to try to do this alone. That feels scary. But like... doable-scary? Not impossible-scary. Which is kind of new.

client_context: A 36-year-old veteran who started heavy drinking after deployment. Views drinking as normal military culture. Wife threatened divorce.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know this probably wasn't how you planned to spend your Tuesday. [pause] There's no agenda here — no checklist I'm working through. I'm just... curious about what's been going on for you. What brings you in?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, uh... my doc said I had to come talk to somebody before he'd clear me. Something about my liver numbers being off. Honestly I feel fine. Been feeling fine. So I'm not really sure what we're supposed to be doing here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the labs flagged something, and part of you is thinking — there might not actually be anything wrong.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, those numbers can be off, right? I've seen guys way worse than me. I still work out, I eat decent. I'm not — I don't know. I'm not what people picture when they say someone has a drinking problem. I hold my shit together.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does that look like to you — someone who actually has a drinking problem?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Like... falling-down drunk every night. Can't hold a job, losing their house or whatever. I've been at the same firm for three years. I show up. [shifts in seat] I drink, yeah. After deployment you drink. That's just what you do. Nobody's handing out medals for sobriety over there, I'll tell you that much.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Drinking was part of the culture. Part of how guys got through it — got through each other.

utterances.speaker: client
