utterances.text: Exactly. And nobody batted an eye then. Now I'm back stateside and suddenly it's — everyone's got something to say. My doctor, my wife, now... no offense... you. Like I'm the problem all of a sudden.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're getting it from every direction and that is exhausting. [pause] And you showed up anyway.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I showed up because my doc basically made it a condition. [short laugh] Let's not make that into some big thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Fair enough. [sits quietly for a moment] You mentioned your wife. Sounds like there's been some tension there.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She... yeah. She's been saying some stuff. I don't — I really don't want to get into that right now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: ...You don't have to. [long pause] I just noticed something shift in you when you said her name.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She... she used the D word. Divorce. Which is... [stops, looks at floor] I keep telling myself she's bluffing. Sarah doesn't bluff. She doesn't do that. So I don't — I don't actually know what she's going to do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That one landed differently. Not like the labs, not like your doctor. That one got in.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She's not... she's not a dramatic person. So when she said it... [exhales slowly, long pause] I can't lose her. I can't lose my kids. I just — I don't know how to be without it. Like I don't know what I do with all the... the noise in my head without having something to turn it down. I don't know how to turn it off.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been carrying something really heavy for a long time. And you've been doing it alone. [pause] That takes a kind of strength that most people never have to find out if they have.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't feel strong. [quiet] I feel... tired, honestly. Like maybe I'm — I don't know. Maybe something's gotta change. I'm not ready to call myself an alcoholic or put a label on it but... I'm here. I'm sitting here. That's gotta count for something, right?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to say back what I heard today, because I don't want to miss anything. You came in because your doc required it — this wasn't your choice. But somewhere in the last hour, something else happened. Your wife, your kids — that's what actually matters to you. And you said it: you're tired. You don't know yet what the path looks like, but you know where you're standing right now isn't where you want to stay. And you're here. That is something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [long pause] ...Yeah. I think I want to come back. See how this goes. I'm not making any promises but — yeah. I think I want to come back.

client_context: A 45-year-old CEO who drinks a bottle of scotch nightly but maintains stellar work performance. Believes they have everything under control. Partner disagrees.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in. I'm Marcus. Coffee's over there if you want — fair warning, it tastes like it's been sitting since 2019, so... probably skip it. Make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Right. So. Look, I'll be straight with you — I've done this before. Three therapists, one of those intensive weekend things in Arizona. I'm only here because my HR director essentially told me this was the alternative to a formal review. So I'm not sure what you're going to tell me that I haven't already heard.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Arizona, huh. So this isn't your first rodeo with any of this. What'd you make of those experiences — the other counselors, the weekend thing?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Waste of time, honestly. Lot of sitting in a circle, people crying about things that happened in fifth grade. No offense to whatever method you use, but... I run a company. I don't have the luxury of spending six hours unpacking my childhood. I've got board meetings. I've got six hundred employees. The drinking — it's just how I decompress. Plenty of people do it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it sounds like those other experiences felt kind of irrelevant to your actual life. Like they weren't built for someone operating at your level.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Yeah. I mean... look, I'm not saying I'm better than anyone in those groups, I'm just saying — my situation is different. The pressure I carry is different. And honestly? I function. I close deals. Last quarter was our best in eight years. Does that sound like someone whose drinking is, uh, 'out of control?'

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Best quarter in eight years — that's real. I'm curious though... what happened at work that got HR's attention? You don't have to sugarcoat it for me.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... there was a client dinner. I said some things that were — I mean, in context they weren't inappropriate, but apparently... one of the junior partners filed something. And I may have been, um. I wasn't at my best that night. But it was one night. One dinner out of — I don't know, thirty, forty client events a year.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It takes something to come here anyway — even with HR giving you a push. A lot of people in your position would've just lawyered up and stonewalled the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well. I'm not... I don't want to be that guy. I've seen executives pull that move and it never ends well. I just — I genuinely don't think I have a problem in the clinical sense. I think I have a demanding life and a habit that happens to be alcohol. There's a difference.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Outside of work — what does the rest of your life look like right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... fine. It's fine. My wife — well, she... she's been sleeping in the guest room for about three months. She says she can't sleep because of the smell, she says. Or because I'm up late. I don't know. We don't really talk about it. We don't really talk about much lately, if I'm honest.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Three months is a long time to be that far apart from someone. Sounds lonely.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. It is. I keep telling myself it'll sort itself out, that I'll ease up after this next push at work, but... she asked me last month if I thought we were going to be okay. And I didn't have an answer. I didn't have anything to say. That scared me more than the HR thing, honestly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me try to piece together what I'm hearing. You've got a career that by most measures is exceptional — best quarter in eight years, six hundred people counting on you. And at the same time, there's this incident at work that shook you enough to show up here instead of fighting it. Your wife is sleeping three rooms away and you didn't know what to tell her when she asked about your future. And underneath all of it, there's a voice that keeps saying 'after this next push, I'll deal with it.' That's... a lot to be carrying.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you lay it out like that... I don't know. I've been telling myself a story for a while now. That I'm handling it. That anyone would drink if they had my job. But the 'after this next push' thing — my wife actually said those exact words back to me once. Called it my 'after' problem. Said I've been saying 'after' for four years.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Four years is a long time to live in 'after.' If something did shift — not for HR, not for your company — just for you... what would you actually want to look different?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'd want to sleep. Actual sleep, not just... passing out. I'd want to wake up and not already feel like I'm behind before I've done anything. And I'd want... I'd like to be able to sit in the same room as my wife without it being this thing hanging over us. I miss her. I miss being — I used to be kind of funny, you know? She used to laugh at my stuff. That's been gone for a while.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The funny guy who made his wife laugh — that's not gone. That's still you, underneath a habit that's been doing a lot of heavy lifting for a very long time. What you just described — real sleep, being present, being in the room with her — that's not a small thing to want. That's everything.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it kind of is, isn't it. I don't — I'm not going to pretend I walked in here ready to turn my whole life upside down. But maybe... maybe there's something worth actually looking at here. I'm willing to try. I think.

client_context: A 45-year-old CEO who drinks a bottle of scotch nightly but maintains stellar work performance. Believes they have everything under control. Partner disagrees.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know this probably wasn't how you planned to spend your Wednesday. There's no agenda here — I'm not going to lecture you or tell you what to do. So let me just ask: what's your sense of why you're here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My HR director set this up. There was a... situation at work, and now apparently everyone's acting like I need to come talk to someone. I'm here because I was told to be here. That's the full story.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You were told to come, and part of you is probably wondering what the point of this even is.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Frankly? Yes. I run a company. Forty-three people depend on me. I handle more before nine in the morning than most people do all week. So the idea that I need to come sit here and... talk about my feelings, or whatever this is — it feels a little... I don't know. Redundant.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're someone who solves problems, moves fast, keeps things running. This kind of conversation feels like it's below what you need to be dealing with right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's not that I'm above it, it's just — I handle things. That's what I do. The situation at work, and I want to be clear, it has been blown completely out of proportion. It was one moment. One. I've been performing at the top of my field for over twenty years without a single incident.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me what happened.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: There was a board call. I was... sharper than I should have been with one of the directors. Said something I wouldn't have said on a normal day. I'd had a rough night — didn't sleep well, came in running on empty. These things happen to everyone. It's not indicative of anything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A rough night. I'm curious — when you say that, what does a rough night actually look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... I usually have a drink or two to wind down. Maybe more. The job doesn't stop when I walk through the door — I'm still running scenarios, thinking through problems, my brain just doesn't quit. The scotch quiets it down enough that I can actually sleep. That's not — look, that's not a problem, that's just a coping mechanism. Half of corporate America does the same thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the drinking isn't the problem — it's actually the solution. The only thing that reliably turns your brain off at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. Exactly. My partner doesn't get that. She thinks I should just, I don't know, meditate. Do yoga. But she's not carrying forty people's livelihoods. She doesn't understand what that weight is like every single day. She sees the bottle and jumps straight to a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds lonely. Carrying all of that, and feeling like the people closest to you can't quite see what it actually costs you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... yeah. Yeah, it is. It's... look, I didn't come in here planning to say something like that. But there's a lot of nights where I'm just sitting there — house is quiet, everyone's asleep — and I'm still... running. Glass in hand, staring at nothing. I didn't think that was something worth mentioning to anyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me reflect back what I'm hearing. You've built something real — a company, a family, a reputation. And somewhere along the way, scotch became the only actual off switch you have. And at the same time, it's starting to cost you things — the board call, your partner's concern, those quiet nights that don't feel quiet anymore. I'm not drawing conclusions. But I'm curious what you make of all that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've been telling myself it's fine because the numbers are still good. Revenue's up, no one's quit, clients are happy. But... the other morning I woke up and my hands were shaking a little before I had my coffee. I told myself it was fatigue. Too much stress. But... I knew. I think some part of me knew exactly what it was.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took real honesty — to notice something like that and then say it out loud to a stranger. What did it feel like to push that observation to the side every morning?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Terrifying. It felt terrifying, if I'm honest. Because if that's real, then I have to actually deal with it. And I've never — I've always known what to do. About everything. That's who I am. And this is the first time I genuinely don't know. I don't know what comes next.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've spent twenty years solving hard problems that other people walked away from. And right now, this is the hardest one — not because you don't have what it takes, but because it's yours. So I want to ask you: what would it actually mean for your life if you tackled this one the same way you tackle everything else?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It would mean... maybe not waking up at three in the morning feeling like I'm made of lead. Maybe actually being present at dinner instead of just counting down until I can pour a glass. My son's twelve. He's not going to be twelve for long. Maybe it means being there for that — actually there, not just... in the room. I don't know. Maybe that's possible. Maybe.

client_context: A 42-year-old construction worker who drinks a six-pack every night. Referred by his doctor after abnormal liver tests. Thinks the doctor is overreacting.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know this wasn't your idea, so I appreciate you showing up. What I'd like to do is just... hear from you. In your own words — what's going on from your perspective?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Look, I'll be straight with you — my doctor told me I had to come here or she'd keep bugging me. My liver numbers were off or whatever. But honestly? I think she's blowing it way out of proportion. I've been drinking the same amount for twenty years. I work hard, I provide for my family. It's just how I unwind.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you've been doing this a long time, it works for you, and someone else decided there was a problem. That feels unfair, maybe.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly. I mean — unfair is one word for it. I've got guys on my crew who drink way more than me. I'm functional. I show up every single day. You know how many guys on a job site don't even make it in half the time? I'm not that guy. Never been that guy.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You hold yourself to a high standard — showing up, doing the job. That clearly matters to you. I want to ask you something directly, and I hope that's okay. Those liver numbers your doctor mentioned — what exactly did she tell you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She said... um. She said they were elevated. Significantly elevated, her exact words. And that if I didn't make changes it could turn into something more serious. Cirrhosis, she mentioned. Which — I mean, that's for alcoholics. I'm not an alcoholic. I've never missed a day of work because of drinking.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She used the word cirrhosis. That's a heavy word to hear sitting in a doctor's office.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. It... yeah. I kind of shut down after that, honestly. Wasn't really listening to the rest of what she said. I figured she was just trying to scare me into something. But then I couldn't sleep that night. Kept thinking about it. Which pissed me off.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You couldn't let it go. Even though part of you really wanted to.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My dad had liver problems. He, uh... he died at sixty-one. And I'm forty-two now, and I keep thinking — that's not that far off, you know? I've got kids. I've got a daughter who's fifteen. I'm not trying to check out early.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Losing your dad that way, watching that — and now getting similar news yourself. You don't want that story to repeat. What would it mean to your daughter if things went in a different direction?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She'd be... I don't know. She's at that age where she acts like she doesn't need me, right? But she does. I coach her soccer team on weekends. That's my thing — that's the one thing that's just ours. I can't imagine not being there for that. Like, that one hits different.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think something important is sitting here. You came in today skeptical — you don't see yourself as having a problem, and you get to decide that. But there's also this other part of you that couldn't sleep after hearing the word cirrhosis. That's watching what happened to your dad. That's picturing your daughter on that soccer field and needing to be there. Both of those things are real at the same time.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I mean. I haven't said it like that but... yeah. That's pretty much it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Given everything you just shared — what do you think you're actually willing to look at here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm not saying I'm gonna quit cold turkey or whatever. But... maybe I could cut back. See if the numbers go down. Like, maybe not every single night. Or not a full six. I don't know if I can actually do that but... it might be worth trying. Maybe.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a real shift from where you walked in today. You're not writing this off anymore — you're actually thinking about what you could do differently. That takes something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I don't want to be dramatic about it. But I also don't want to be stupid. If my liver is telling me something, maybe I should actually listen this time. I just — I've never really thought about it this way before. Nobody's ever asked me about my dad.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in thinking this was a waste of time. And somewhere in this conversation you connected drinking to your dad, to your liver results, to your daughter on that soccer field wanting her father there. That's not a small thing. Before we finish — what's one realistic step you could take this week? Not perfect, just real.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe skip a night. See how that actually feels. And... the doctor gave me this printout about my results. I kind of threw it in the glove box. Haven't looked at it. Maybe I should actually read the thing.

client_context: A 16-year-old whose parents found empty bottles hidden in their room. Brought to counseling against their will. Scared but trying to act tough.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know this probably wasn't your idea, so I want you to know — you don't have to pretend to be okay with being here. We can just... start wherever you are. What's it been like since you finished the program?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's whatever. I mean, it was fine I guess. People kept telling me I had a problem and I just... sat there. Did what they wanted.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you went through it, did what was expected — but it didn't really feel like it was for you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. Like, my parents freaked out, the judge said go, so I went. Whatever. Doesn't mean anything was actually... wrong.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I hear that. And I'm not here to tell you there's something wrong with you. But I am curious — you said it doesn't mean anything was wrong. What would 'something being wrong' even look like to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. Like... I don't know. Drinking until you black out every night? Losing your job? I'm sixteen, I don't have a job to lose. It was just... parties. Everyone does it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Everyone does it. And still, somehow, you're the one sitting here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I know. That's the part I can't— I keep thinking about that. Like why me. My friends were there too and they just... went home.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds really lonely. Feeling like you're carrying something your friends just... walked away from.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. Kind of. My parents won't even look at me the same. My mom cried. I hate that she cried. I never wanted — that wasn't supposed to happen.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It matters to you. What your mom thinks, what this has done to your family — even if part of you has been acting like it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm not acting. I just... I didn't know how to— I don't know. Yeah. It matters. Obviously it matters, she's my mom.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Can I ask you something a little harder? When you think about the next year — school, your family, all of it — what are you most scared of?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That... um. That it doesn't get better. That I already screwed it up too much and like, no matter what I do now it's just — this is just who I am now. The kid who got arrested. That's it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a heavy thing to carry — the fear that one thing has already decided your whole story. And I want to reflect something back to you: the fact that you're sitting here, that you finished that program, that you hate seeing your mom cry — none of that sounds like someone who's already given up.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I don't know. Maybe. I just don't want to be that guy, you know? Like, my older cousin went down that road and he's just — he's nowhere now. I don't want that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me pull together what I'm hearing. You came in today feeling like this wasn't your choice, and maybe nothing was even really wrong. But somewhere in this conversation, something shifted — you talked about your mom, about your cousin, about not wanting to be that guy. That's not nothing. That's actually a lot of reasons.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... yeah. I don't — I'm not saying I have it all figured out. But like. I don't want to just keep... doing nothing, I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's enough to start with. You don't need to have it figured out. What would feel like one small thing — just one — that would make next week look even a little different than last month?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... actually talking to my mom. Like for real, not just saying sorry and going to my room. I think she deserves that. I think I owe her that much.

client_context: A 20-year-old star athlete whose performance has been slipping due to partying. Coach gave an ultimatum. Torn between team loyalty and social life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know this isn't exactly how most guys want to spend a Wednesday afternoon. [pause] So — what brings you in?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... honestly? My girlfriend basically told me if I don't do this she's done. And my coach has been on my case, so... I don't really feel like I had much of a choice coming here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So a couple of pretty important people in your life are worried about you. [pause] What's your take on all of it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I think they're overreacting, honestly. Like yeah, I drink at parties, but it's college, you know? Everyone does it. I'm not like — I'm not some alcoholic or whatever. That's not what's happening here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're not seeing it the way they're seeing it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. I mean — okay, my numbers have been down a little. My forty time slipped two tenths. But that could be anything. Could be sleep, could be the hip I tweaked in October. It doesn't have to be the drinking. Nobody can actually prove that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's this gap between how you're seeing it and how they're seeing it, and that's... frustrating. Like you got pushed into a room you didn't ask to walk into. And you've been here before — counseling — and it didn't help.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Twice. Both times it was just someone telling me what I should and shouldn't do. Like they already had the answer before I even said anything. And it didn't — nothing changed. So I'm just... [pause] I don't know why this time is supposed to be different.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been through this twice, it hasn't worked, and you still showed up today. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... [pause] I don't want to lose her. Kayla. And I don't want to get kicked off the team. Like those are actual real things that could happen, and I — yeah. I guess that's why I'm here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me more about that — the team, Kayla. What do those actually mean to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Football is... I've been playing since I was seven. My dad never missed a game, not one. It's like — it's not just a sport, it's who I am, it's my whole family. And Kayla, she's been with me since sophomore year of high school. She's the only person who like... actually gets me. She doesn't just see the athlete. She sees me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Football is tied up in who you are, your dad, your whole family — it's not just a performance metric. And Kayla sees something in you that most people miss.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [long pause] And I think... she's scared. She doesn't say it like that but the way she looks at me after a night out — it's not even anger anymore. It's like she's just... tired. And that's somehow worse than if she was yelling at me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something shifted in how you just described that. [pause] What do you think is actually at stake here — for you, not for them?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... if I keep going the way I'm going, I lose all of it. The team, Kayla, all of it. And then what am I? Just some guy who used to be good at football and didn't know when to stop. That's — that's not who I want to be.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That version of yourself — the one who keeps all of it — what does he look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: He shows up. Like actually shows up, not dragging himself through practice with a headache. He finishes his senior year strong, maybe gets drafted, or at least goes out with his head up. And Kayla — she's proud of him. She's not worried all the time. [pause] That sounds really different from right now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to bring this together. You came in because people pushed you here, and part of you was ready to write this off like the last two times. But somewhere in this conversation something else showed up — a guy who knows exactly what matters to him. Football, your dad, Kayla. And you can see pretty clearly where the road goes if nothing changes. That's not a small thing to sit with.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. [pause] It's not. [long pause] I think I've been... avoiding thinking about it that way. Like if I actually look at it, then I have to do something about it. And that's — honestly that's scarier than just not looking.

client_context: A 42-year-old construction worker who drinks a six-pack every night. Referred by his doctor after abnormal liver tests. Thinks the doctor is overreacting.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Last time we met, things were already pretty tense. And you mentioned this week was rough. I want to hear what happened — in your own words.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't even know why I keep coming back here, honestly. My doctor sends another letter, my wife forwards it to me at work like I'm a kid who needs to be reminded, and now I'm sitting here again. I'm not a drunk. I work sixty hours a week. I support my whole family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You feel like everyone's decided something about you — and nobody asked.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Twenty years in construction. I show up, I do the work, I come home. A six-pack at night — that's how I decompress. That's what guys do. My father did it, his father did it. Nobody sent them to a counselor.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You mentioned there was a setback this week. Tell me what happened.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I tried, okay? Monday I had like three beers. Tuesday same thing. Then Wednesday we had a bad pour on a slab — whole section had to be redone — and I just... I don't know. I ended up drinking more than usual that night. A lot more. Whatever, it was one night.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You cut back two nights in a row on your own. Without anyone standing over you. That actually took something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. I guess I did. But Wednesday undid all of it, so. What's the point of counting two good days when the third one blows up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're writing off Monday and Tuesday because of Wednesday. Like they don't count unless the streak is perfect.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Maybe. I don't know. It's just — look, my back's been bad since spring, like a real problem, and by the time I get home I'm done. I'm physically done. And I need something to take the edge off or I can't even sleep. Is that so hard to understand?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The pain is real and I'm not dismissing that. I do want to ask about something else though — when you got those new liver results, what actually went through your head when you read them?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... I didn't read it right away. But my wife did, and she got real quiet. Like that quiet where you know something's wrong. The numbers went up from last time and the doctor used the word... um. Cirrhosis. So I looked it up. I probably shouldn't have looked it up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That word landed hard.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: There was a guy on a site I worked maybe eight years ago. He had it. He got yellow — like actually yellow, his eyes and everything. He was... he was gone inside two years. I'm forty-two. I've got a kid in high school. I keep thinking about that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're thinking about your son. What does it mean to you when you put it in those terms — being there for him?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want to see him graduate. I want to... I don't know. I haven't really let myself think about it that way. Like, actually picture not being there. That's — that's a different thing than some doctor's letter.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something shifted just now when you said that. This stopped being about your doctor's opinion.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... yeah, I think so. I don't know if I can just quit cold or whatever. I don't even know what that looks like for someone like me. But maybe — maybe I could do it different than I have been. I don't know where you'd even start.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think it matters. You came in today ready to push back — and you had every reason to feel that way. But you also tried to cut back this week on your own, without anyone making you. You came back here even after a hard Wednesday. And when you think about your son, something becomes real that the medical stuff alone couldn't touch. That's worth paying attention to.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it is. I'm not promising anything crazy. But... yeah. I think I want to figure this out.

client_context: A 32-year-old ER nurse who started drinking heavily during the pandemic. Feels guilty but says it's the only way to decompress after traumatic shifts.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in. I'm Marcus. Grab a seat wherever — I promise the chair by the window is not cursed, despite what the last guy said. So, this is kind of a walk-in situation for you, yeah? What's going on?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um. Yeah. I mean, I'm here because I kind of... have to be. Court thing. I got a DUI a few months back and this is part of the — the thing they want me to do. The program. So.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay, so the court's got a foot in the door. That makes sense. I'm not gonna pretend that's a super fun reason to be sitting here. But I'm curious — now that you're actually in the room, what's going through your head about all this?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I feel like this is... I don't know, overkill? Like, one incident doesn't mean I have a drinking problem. I work insane hours as an ER nurse, I've been doing that for like six years, and sometimes you just — you blow off steam. That's it. That's all it was.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Six years in the ER. And somewhere in there, blowing off steam started looking like getting behind the wheel.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I wasn't — okay, I wasn't wasted. I was... I was over the limit, technically, but I was fine. I've driven in way worse shape after night shifts without sleeping, honestly. Which, I know how that sounds.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You caught yourself there — 'I know how that sounds.' That actually takes a certain kind of self-awareness, even if it doesn't feel like it right now. You're not sitting here telling me everything's fine. There's something you're wrestling with.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. A little bit. I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me about the shifts. What does a bad night in the ER actually look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... okay so during the pandemic it was just — we had people dying in the hallways. Like, literally. We were triaging people and there weren't enough vents and you're just... you're making calls that no one should have to make. And then you go home and you're supposed to just, what, watch Netflix? I couldn't sleep. I still can't sometimes. The drinking actually helped with that, at least at first.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: At first it worked. It quieted things down enough that you could get some rest, feel something other than all of that. And then at some point... it stopped being just about sleep.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I don't... I don't even really notice when I started needing more of it. Like, a glass of wine became half a bottle became — I don't know. And I kept telling myself I was fine because I was still showing up to work, still doing my job. But there were a couple times this past year where I came in and I was... I wasn't all the way there. And I knew it. I knew it and I still went in.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a heavy thing to carry around. Knowing and still going in. What does that mean to you — as a nurse, as someone who clearly takes that work seriously?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It means I'm... it means I'm not the person I thought I was, maybe. I went into nursing because I actually wanted to help people. Like for real, not just — not just as a thing to say. And now I'm... I'm scared that I'm going to make a mistake that hurts someone because of this. That's the thing I don't let myself think about too much.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The thing you're most afraid of is hurting someone in your care. And you named it out loud just now, even though it's the thing you've been pushing away. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... yeah. I mean, I've been doing this long enough that muscle memory can cover for a lot. But I've noticed things. Little things. I blanked on a medication calculation last month and I had to double-check myself three times. I never used to do that. And I just — I don't know how much of that is exhaustion and how much is... this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull together what I'm hearing, see if I've got it right. You came in today because the court said you had to, and part of you felt like this was an overreaction to one bad night. But as we've been talking, something else has been surfacing — this picture of someone who went through real trauma during the pandemic, who found something that helped her survive it, and who's now watching that same thing start to chip away at the one thing that matters most to her. Her ability to actually take care of people. Does that fit?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
...

Yeah. That's... that fits better than I wanted it to.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So knowing all that — what do you think you want to do with it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I really don't. But I think... I think I need to actually look at this. Not just for the court stuff. I can't keep — I can't keep showing up halfway, you know? That's not who I want to be.

client_context: A 24-year-old PhD student who has been drinking to manage thesis stress and imposter syndrome. Advisor noticed declining work quality.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in. I know you're between classes, so I want to make sure we use the time well. Can you tell me in your own words what brought you here today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... yeah. I mean, I had to go to the ER on Friday night. I'm fine, physically — they said I was fine. But they kind of... recommended I talk to someone. So. Here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You showed up. That matters more than you might think right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess. I don't know, I feel like I'm making a bigger deal out of it than it is. It was just one bad night. I've been really stressed with my thesis and I just... drank more than I should have.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What's the thesis stress been like lately?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... god, it's a lot. I'm in my third year and my advisor basically told me last week that my last chapter draft wasn't up to standard. And I've been feeling like everyone else in my cohort just gets it and I'm the one who's... faking it, you know? Like I don't actually belong there and eventually someone's going to figure that out.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So there's this feeling that you're somehow behind, not measuring up — and the drinking's been a way to turn that off for a little while.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, yeah, but — it's not like I'm some kind of alcoholic. I go days without it. It's just when the anxiety gets really bad at night, it's the only thing that actually works. My brain just won't shut up otherwise. I've tried everything else.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What have you tried?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Journaling, meditation apps, I ran for like two weeks straight — and then defense prep got intense and I just stopped. Nothing sticks. The drinking is at least... immediate. It works. Until it doesn't. Until Friday.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's been this reliable shortcut for a long time — and Friday was the first time it backfired in a way that you couldn't just shake off.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... waking up in the hospital and having to text my advisor that I missed our morning meeting — that was a really bad feeling. Like, that's the thing I'm most scared of. Losing his respect. Losing my spot in the program.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The program, the research — that clearly means something real to you. What does it look like if you actually get to the other side of this?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want to finish. Genuinely. I didn't come this far to... I picked this topic because I actually care about it — climate adaptation policy. People make fun of academics but like, I think this work matters. I just don't know how to get from where I am right now to... that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me make sure I'm understanding this right. You're someone who genuinely cares about your research — this isn't just a credential, it means something to you. You've been carrying a lot of anxiety about not being good enough, and drinking became the thing that made that bearable. And now, after Friday, there's a part of you starting to wonder if that strategy is actually putting the thing you care most about at risk.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you say it like that... yeah. Yeah, that's kind of exactly it. I've been so focused on just surviving week to week that I haven't really let myself think about it that way.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What feels like one thing — even something small — that might look different going forward?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I need to actually get real support for the anxiety. Not just white-knuckle it alone at midnight. And maybe actually be honest with my advisor about how much I'm struggling instead of just disappearing when things get bad. He probably already knows something's wrong anyway.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Those aren't small things. That's two really clear-eyed insights — that the anxiety needs real support, not just management, and that isolating from your advisor is making things harder, not easier. You came in here rushed, not sure this was worth your time. And you're already thinking about what comes next. That says something about you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I still have a methods section I've been avoiding for two weeks. But yeah. I think I actually want to figure this out. Not just survive it.

client_context: A 33-year-old social media influencer whose entire social life revolves around drinking. Multiple friends have expressed concern. Insists it's just her lifestyle.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So... you came back. I'm really glad you're here, especially after everything you mentioned at the end of last session. I'd love to hear — what has this week actually been like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? It's been... okay, it's been kind of a lot. But like, don't read too much into that. It was just — you know how it goes. Events, people, cameras everywhere, and then... I don't know. A whole thing happened. But I'm fine. I'm always fine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A lot happened... and somewhere underneath 'I'm fine,' I'm hearing something else. Something that made this week feel heavier than usual.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean — okay, yeah. There was this thing at the brand launch on Friday. And I... look, it happens to everyone, right? Like, celebrities post stuff like that all the time and nobody makes it a whole situation. I just — I don't know why my manager had to call me about it like I was some kind of liability.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What was it like, getting that call from your manager?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Embarrassing? No — annoying. It was annoying. Because it's like, I know how to handle myself. I have a brand. I have built something. Six years. And she's acting like one video is going to, I don't know, tank my entire career. Which is dramatic. Incredibly dramatic.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've built something real — six years, a whole identity, relationships, a community of people who follow you. And then in one moment, someone you trust is questioning all of it. That has to sting, even when you don't want it to.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... yeah. Yeah, it does. I just — I hate that she saw it before I did. Like, I didn't even remember posting it. I thought I was just having fun and then I wake up and there's three hundred comments and my DMs are just... [trails off] ...it's fine. I deleted it. Problem solved.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You didn't remember posting it. [pause]

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... No. I didn't. [long pause] I hate saying that out loud. That sounds — I don't know what it sounds like, but it sounds bad. It sounds like the kind of thing people say right before they, like, go on Dr. Phil or something. And I'm not that person.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like someone who's hurting and doesn't quite know what to do with that yet. You don't have to make it make sense right now. [pause] Can I ask — who is Jasmine when the cameras aren't on?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Ha. God. Um... [laughs softly, then stops] That's actually a really good question. I'm still fun? I'm — look, I like who I am. I like my life. Not everything has to be this deep psychological excavation. Some people just live at a faster pace and that's okay. That's allowed.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just try to reflect back what I'm hearing across today, if that's okay. You came in after a week that really shook you — a moment you don't fully remember, a manager who's worried, friends who've said something, a post you had to delete. And alongside all of that, you clearly care deeply about the life you've built and the person you've become. Both of those things are sitting here in the room with us right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you say it like that it sounds... I mean, okay. Listed out like that it does sound like a lot. But you could do that with anyone's week, right? You could take literally anyone's Wednesday and frame it as a crisis. That doesn't mean it is one.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm. And if it were a cry for help — just hypothetically — what would you want someone to actually hear?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... [quiet for a moment] I guess I'd just want someone to not make me feel like I'm broken. Like — I'm not broken. I'm just tired. I think I'm actually just really, really tired. And I don't know when that happened.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're not broken. And being tired — tired of holding everything together, tired of performing, tired of waking up and not quite knowing what happened the night before — that's not weakness. That's actually a kind of honesty. And it took courage to say it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Okay, now you sound like a poster in a yoga studio. [laughs] But... yeah. I don't know. I've always just called it being busy. Busy sounds better than tired. Busy sounds like you're winning. But maybe it's the same thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it feel like to give yourself just a little more room — even a little — to be something other than busy?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Probably terrifying. Like, my whole thing is that I'm always on, always somewhere, always doing something. But also... maybe nice? I genuinely don't know. That's a weird answer but it's the truest one I've got right now.

client_context: An 18-year-old referred by school counselor after being caught drinking at a school event. Feels singled out since 'literally everyone drinks'.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in. I'm Dr. Reyes. You can grab that chair, whichever one's comfortable. No pressure to sit a certain way or anything like that. I just want you to know — nothing you say in here leaves this room, with a couple of exceptions I can tell you about if you want. But mostly, this is just... a conversation.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Okay. Um. Cool.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So what's your sense of why you're here today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Because my school counselor, like, made it happen. I didn't — I'm not here voluntarily, if that's what you're asking. They caught me at the fall formal with a flask and now suddenly I'm the problem kid who has to go to therapy. Which is... whatever. It's fine. I'm just saying, literally half the people there were drinking and I'm the one who got pulled out.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It feels really unfair. Like you got singled out when everyone else was doing the same thing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. And now I'm the one sitting in a therapist's office like I'm some kind of... I don't know, like I have a problem. My parents are freaking out, my counselor keeps emailing them, and I just... I don't see what the big deal is. It was one night.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me a little more about what drinking is usually like for you — like in your friend group, what does that look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... it's normal. We hang out, sometimes there's drinks at parties. It's not like we're, um, doing it every day or whatever. It's just — that's kind of how it goes on weekends. Everyone does it. My older sister did it. My parents did it when they were my age, I guarantee you. So I don't really get why I'm being treated like some kind of alcoholic.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're not an alcoholic for drinking at a party. And I'll be honest — you're right that it's really common at your age. What I'm actually noticing is that even though you didn't want to be here, you're being pretty straight with me. That takes something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I mean, I'm not gonna lie to you. That seems pointless.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I appreciate that. So — and you don't have to have a good answer — but is there any part of this whole situation that's been bothering you? Not necessarily the drinking itself, just... any of it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I guess I hate that my mom cried. That was — I didn't expect that. She didn't yell or anything, she just sat there and cried and that was actually way worse. And I don't know, maybe I feel kind of bad about it? But also I still think everyone is overreacting.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So there are two things happening at once — part of you is like, this isn't a big deal, everyone does it. And another part of you saw your mom cry and that actually got to you. Both of those things can be true at the same time.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I guess that's... kind of it. Like I'm not trying to hurt her. That's not — that's not the point of any of this. I just want to have a normal life and not be treated like a child.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would a normal life look like for you — like, what do you actually want it to feel like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want... I don't know, I want to hang out with my friends and not have my parents watching every single thing I do. But also I kind of want them to trust me again? Because right now my mom barely looks at me and that's — that sucks. I didn't think it would be this bad. Maybe I should've thought more about, like, where I was doing it. School was probably not the smartest call.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing. You came in feeling frustrated — like you got caught when everyone else was doing the same thing and that wasn't fair. And that's still part of it. But you also care a lot about your relationship with your mom, more than you maybe expected. And you're starting to think that some of the choices around where and when might be worth looking at — not because drinking is automatically a crisis, but because some of this has cost you something that matters to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... when you put it like that it kind of makes sense. Like, yeah. I don't want to lose my mom's trust over something that was just supposed to be fun. That's a really bad trade.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just said something really important — you figured out on your own what the trade-off actually was. Nobody handed you that. That's you thinking it through. So I want to ask: what feels like one small thing you could do differently that would start to rebuild that trust with her?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe just... talk to her? Like actually talk, not just say sorry to get out of trouble. Tell her I heard her and I'm not trying to make her feel like that again. I think that might actually help. I don't know, I've never really done that before but... yeah. Maybe I could try that.

client_context: A 55-year-old who lost their spouse 8 months ago and has been drinking to numb the pain. Isolated from friends and family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for making time today — I know you're squeezed between classes, so I want to be respectful of that. What brings you in?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My doctor sent me, basically. My lab work came back with some numbers that weren't right — liver enzymes, she said. I don't... I mean, I've been under a lot of stress. I lost my husband eight months ago, so. I think that's all it is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Eight months. You've been carrying a tremendous amount of grief — and you're still carrying it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I manage. I have a glass of wine in the evenings, sometimes two, to help me sleep. That's not... I mean, that's not unusual. Lots of people do that. My doctor's being a little dramatic, I think.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When she told you about those results, what went through your mind in that moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Not much. I thought, okay, I'm 55, things fall apart. And... I don't know. Part of me thought maybe it doesn't matter that much anymore. Which sounds terrible to say out loud. I don't know why I said that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound terrible — it sounds like someone whose reason to take care of herself is tied up in a person who isn't here anymore.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Yeah, that's... Robert always made me eat breakfast. Just stood there until I did, every single morning for thirty-one years. Silly thing to think about. [quiet laugh] Sorry. That has nothing to do with anything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That has everything to do with everything. And — you almost didn't come in today, but you did. That took something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I sat in the parking lot for like ten minutes. My daughter has been worried — she calls, and I can hear it in her voice, and I just... I don't want her checking on her mother every other day. She's 28. She's got her own life to live.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it mean to her — if she knew you were genuinely okay?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She'd just... live. She'd stop hovering. I want that for her. But I'm not okay, really. I know I'm not. I've been — I've been pretty alone with all of it, and the evenings are the worst. The house is so quiet.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The quiet is unbearable, and the drinking turns the volume down on it. And somewhere you know it's not actually helping — it's just... postponing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Robert would hate this. He wouldn't be angry — he never got angry — he'd just sit down next to me and... [voice breaks] I'm sorry. Sorry. I don't usually — I don't do this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Don't apologize. Please.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I've been avoiding it. The feeling. Because if I actually stop and let myself feel it, it's like... it's too big. The wine just turns the volume down. But the pain's still there, isn't it. It's not going anywhere.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Grief doesn't dissolve — it just waits. But what you just said, right there, is one of the clearest things I've heard in a while: you can see exactly what the drinking is doing and what it isn't doing. That kind of honesty is actually where things can start to shift.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I never thought of it as a... problem problem. I just thought I was coping. But sitting here I think maybe I've been kidding myself for a while now. I've been so alone with it. I pushed people away, I think. My friends stopped calling and I let them.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me pull together what I'm hearing. You came in today — even after sitting in that parking lot — because the people you love are worried, because your body is sending you a warning, and because part of you already knows the drinking isn't touching the grief, it's just delaying it. And you're saying you don't want to keep doing this. That's not a small thing to arrive at in twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I think I actually want to try. I don't know where to start, but... yeah. Robert would want me to try. I know he would.

client_context: A 39-year-old diagnosed with depression who self-medicates with alcohol. Has tried therapy before and dropped out. Skeptical but willing to give it one more try.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in... take your time getting settled. No rush. I know walk-in appointments can feel a little — I don't know — like you're just being shuffled somewhere. I appreciate you coming in. What brought you here today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My doctor. Uh, Dr. Reyes. She flagged something on a screening and said I should come talk to somebody. I've... done therapy before, so I know what this is. Didn't really help. But she keeps bringing it up every appointment, so. Here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you're here more because she wouldn't let it go than because you really wanted to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean — yeah, basically. No offense. I just... last time I did this I went like six sessions and felt like I was talking in circles. Nothing changed. So I stopped going. And then life got busy and I just — yeah. I don't really know what you're supposed to do with me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What do you think Dr. Reyes is most worried about? Like what do you imagine she sees when she looks at that screening?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Probably the drinking. She asked how many drinks I have a week and I told her and she got that look, you know? That — that doctor face. It's not like I'm falling down drunk or whatever. I hold a job. I pay my bills. I drink to unwind after work. I don't see how that's different from anyone else.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you're keeping it together. Functioning. And at the same time... you kind of already knew what her face was going to look like before she even made it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah, I knew she wasn't going to love the number. [pause] Look, this year's been rough, okay? The depression's been — it's been bad. So maybe I've been leaning on it a bit more than usual. But I'm not an alcoholic. I know what that looks like. That's not me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You said that before I even asked. I notice that. There's a kind of self-awareness in that — knowing where the line is, or at least... where you're afraid it might be heading. A lot of people can't do that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just — I don't like labels. My dad was a drinker. Like a real drinker, the kind you see in movies. And I swore I'd never be that. [quieter] But I guess sometimes I wonder if I'm more like him than I want to admit. I don't know. That's a weird thing to say to a stranger.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's not weird at all. That took something to say out loud. Can I ask — the depression and the drinking, how do those two things fit together for you? Like... which one came first, or does that even matter at this point?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Depression's been around since I was like... seventeen, eighteen. On and off. The drinking — I started doing it more when things got dark again, a few years back. Like I'd come home and everything just felt heavy, you know? Just... crushing. And a couple drinks and the edge came off. I could finally breathe. It became the thing I looked forward to at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The one thing that actually gave you some relief. Some quiet from all that weight.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [long pause] And I know that's not... I'm not stupid, I know alcohol makes depression worse in the long run. I've read about it. But in the moment it's the only thing that actually works. Therapy didn't. Meds — I tried two different ones and they made me feel like a zombie. So what am I supposed to do? Just... sit in it?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you've tried. More than once. Therapy, medication — things that were supposed to help — and they either didn't work or took something from you in the process. And through all of that, the drinking kept showing up for you, at least in the short run. And now you're sitting in another therapy office, probably wondering why this time would be any different.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you put it like that... yeah. That's — yeah. [exhales slowly] I'm just tired, man. I'm really, really tired. I don't want to be sitting in one of these chairs still doing this when I'm fifty.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would not doing this at fifty look like? If something actually shifted — what's the version of yourself you're picturing when you say that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know... just waking up and not immediately dreading the day, I guess. Actually wanting things again. I used to paint — nothing serious, just for myself, like on weekends. I haven't touched it in almost two years. I think I'd want that back. Feeling like there's a point. Like I'm not just... getting through.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That picture is still there. You just described it in real detail — the mornings, the painting, the feeling that things matter. You've been carrying that whole time, underneath everything else. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I didn't... huh. [small laugh] Yeah. Maybe. I'm not making any promises or anything. But... I think I could come back next week. See how it goes.

client_context: A 32-year-old ER nurse who started drinking heavily during the pandemic. Feels guilty but says it's the only way to decompress after traumatic shifts.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in. I know you mentioned you're tight on time, so I really appreciate you making space for this. What brings you in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? My friend basically cornered me and said I had to come. She thinks I have a... problem. I don't know. I've just been really stressed. It's not like I'm some — I don't know. I'm fine. I just figured I'd come so she'd stop worrying.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Part of you came because you care about your friend. And maybe there's another part that's not quite sure this is even necessary.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean... yeah. Look, I'm an ER nurse. Twelve-hour shifts. You have no idea what that's like — watching people die, sometimes multiple people in one shift, and then you just go home and you're supposed to what, make dinner and go to sleep? I need something to come down from that. Wine helps me sleep. That's literally it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds incredibly heavy to carry. What's it been like working in the ER over the last few years?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... god, I don't even know where to start. The pandemic just — it broke something. We were short-staffed, people were terrified, we couldn't do anything for half of them, and we just kept showing up. Every single day. I'd drive home and I couldn't stop seeing faces. I still do sometimes. The drinking... it quiets everything. And I know that sounds bad but I don't — I don't know what else to do anymore. I've tried everything else. I really have.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're exhausted in a way that goes really deep. And the drinking has been the one thing that gives you some relief from something that was — there's no softer word for it — traumatic.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it is. I just... I don't see how stopping would help. The trauma doesn't go away if I stop drinking. I'd just be drowning without the life raft. I honestly don't know how to do this job without it anymore. That's a terrible thing to say but it's true.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It takes real honesty to say that out loud. A lot of people wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't feel honest, I feel... scared, actually. Because lately I've been slipping up at work. Little things — forgetting to chart, missing a handoff. Last week I almost gave the wrong dosage. I caught it. But... that scared me more than anything has in a long time.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does it mean to you that you caught it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That I'm still... in there somewhere. That I still care. I didn't become a nurse to hurt people — I did it because I wanted to help. That's what makes this so hard, you know? I care so much that I think it kind of... broke me. And now I'm scared I'm going to hurt one of my patients because of how I'm dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That caring is still there — you can still feel it. And it sounds like part of you is worried that the drinking is starting to get in the way of the nurse you know yourself to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I haven't let myself say that before. I kept telling myself it's fine, it's managed, it's not touching my work. But honestly? It is. It's starting to. And that's — that's the line for me. That's the thing I cannot let happen.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If you could picture things being even a little different — what would that look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Just... not needing it. Like, being able to come home after a hard shift and be okay without pouring a glass the second I walk in the door. Being able to sleep. I don't even know if that's possible anymore but — I'd really like that. I would really like to not feel like I need it to function.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's a part of you that still wants that life — where you're not dependent on it to get through the day. That part showed up here today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My friend said the same thing. That I'm still fighting. I didn't believe her but... maybe. Maybe that's why I actually came in instead of just saying I would. I think I'm ready to figure out what the next step is. I don't know what that is, but I want to find out.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in today feeling pushed, rushed, not totally sure this was even for you. And in the last forty-five minutes you named something that genuinely scared you about your work, you connected it back to how much you care about your patients, and you said out loud that you want something different. That's not nothing. Before we wrap up — what's one small thing you'd be willing to try before we meet again?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... look into the EAP through the hospital. I've known about it forever but always thought it was for other people, not me. And maybe actually call my friend. Tell her I came, that it wasn't nothing. Yeah. I think I can do those two things.

client_context: A 27-year-old bartender who drinks after every shift. Recently realized they can't remember the last sober day. Starting to question if this is normal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know this kind of appointment can feel a little different from the usual stuff you see at the VA. What brought you in to talk with me?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, uh... my doctor flagged some stuff on my bloodwork. Liver enzymes or something. She kind of — she suggested I come talk to someone. I figured okay, I'll give it a shot. Honestly not sure what to expect.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your doctor saw something that concerned her, and you followed through and showed up. That matters. What's your sense of what she was worried about?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She thinks it's the drinking. Like, I bartend, so — I mean, I drink after my shifts. That's just the culture, you know? But I've been thinking about it more lately and um... I can't actually remember the last day I didn't have a drink. Which is... that's kind of a weird thing to realize.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a significant thing to notice about yourself. When you say you can't remember the last sober day — what's it like to sit with that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Kind of scary. I thought about it on the drive over and I was trying to go back and I just... couldn't find one. Not in recent memory. It's like it just crept up on me. I didn't notice it happening.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It snuck up on you. What started as part of the job just became something you can't picture your days without.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah and like — I'm 27. That's not... I shouldn't be saying I can't go a day without a drink at 27, right? I keep telling myself it's fine because everyone at work does it, but then I'm here so clearly something is off. I don't know, that's kind of a messed up thing to say out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're already questioning your own reasoning. The 'everyone does it' story is getting harder to sell to yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It is. And that's frustrating because I built my whole social life around that scene. My friends are there, that's where I unwind — but like, what am I even unwinding from? I'm at a bar all day and then I just... stay at the bar. That doesn't actually make any sense when I say it like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That question you just asked yourself — what are you actually unwinding from — what comes up when you sit with it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I think I'm lonely. That sounds dumb but. My girlfriend and I split about a year ago and since then it's just been work, drinks with coworkers, home, work. I used to go hiking. I used to play guitar. I haven't touched it in like eight months.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The guitar's been sitting there... and somewhere along the way, the drinking filled in the space where those things used to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's — that's actually exactly it. God, that's depressing. I used to be someone who did stuff. Now I just pour drinks and drink drinks. I didn't... I didn't realize how much I'd let go.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing, see if I've got it right. You came in because your body is starting to send signals — the labs. You've realized there isn't a sober day you can point to. You've watched the things that used to matter — hiking, music, real connection — kind of fade out. And underneath the habit, there's some genuine loneliness, and a version of yourself you miss. Does that land?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. It does. Hearing it all together like that is — it's a lot. I didn't come in thinking it was this deep. I honestly thought I'd get like a pamphlet or something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in expecting a pamphlet and found something worth actually paying attention to. What would it mean to you to get some of that back — the hiking, the guitar, a day where you feel like yourself?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It would mean a lot. I think I've just been on autopilot. Coasting. I used to have goals, you know? Like actual direction. Maybe I could have that again. I don't know where to start but... I think I actually want to try. That's the first time I've said that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That — right there — is exactly the kind of thing worth building on. You walked in not knowing what to expect, sat with some hard things today, and found something real. I'd like to keep working on this with you. What feels like a realistic first step this week — something small but yours?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... not drinking on my day off. Just to see what that feels like. I haven't done that in a while. It's small but it's something. Yeah. I think I can do that.

client_context: A 45-year-old CEO who drinks a bottle of scotch nightly but maintains stellar work performance. Believes they have everything under control. Partner disagrees.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's good to see you today. I know this week was a rough one. I just want to start by asking... how are you feeling coming in right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm fine. Just — it's been a week, you know? Board meeting went sideways, couple of operational fires. Nothing I haven't dealt with before. Honestly, I'm not sure why my wife keeps insisting I come to these. I don't have a lot of spare time.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been carrying a lot this week — the board, the fires at work — and part of you is questioning whether being here even makes sense right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. Look, I built this company from nothing. Forty-three employees, two hundred million in revenue last year. I think I have a pretty decent handle on managing pressure. I've always managed.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a genuinely remarkable thing you've built. And I want to ask something — take your time with it — when your doctor called with those lab results last week... what went through your mind in that moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: The liver panel? Look, the doctor's being overly cautious, that's his job. I'm not some... I don't look like someone with a problem. I went in for a routine physical. Half the executives I know drink. It goes with the territory. Always has.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The word 'problem' doesn't sit right with you. And at the same time... you came back today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I — yeah. I mean, Sarah — my wife — she basically... she cried. Which is not something she does. She's not like that. And the doctor said the numbers were significantly elevated. His word, significantly. I don't know. It's probably fine but she just... she wouldn't let it go.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When Sarah cried... what was that like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I didn't like it. I haven't seen her like that in... I don't know, years maybe. We've been together eighteen years. She's a strong person. She said something like — 'I don't want to lose you.' And I told her she was being dramatic but... I don't know. It stuck with me more than I expected it to.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Seeing her scared like that landed somewhere the lab results alone didn't quite reach.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I think that's right actually. I keep coming back to her face when she said it. And I've been waking up at three in the morning this week just... lying there staring at the ceiling. Which is not like me at all. I'm usually — I mean I have a drink or two to wind down, always helps me sleep, but this week it's like... something's different. I can't put my finger on it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
