utterances.text: The fact that you can't shake it — that you keep returning to her face, that something in you is unsettled at three in the morning — that tells me something about what actually matters most to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm not trying to be dramatic about this. I've never been that guy. But my dad... he had his first heart attack at fifty-two. I'm forty-five. That's seven years. I don't think I've ever said that out loud before, actually. Connected those two things.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've never let yourself connect those two things before. I'm curious — when you imagine what doing something about this could actually look like for you... what comes up?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... hm. I've never really gone there in my head. I always just told myself I'll deal with it when I have more bandwidth. But... 'later' keeps not arriving, doesn't it. I'm not thirty anymore. I keep thinking — what am I actually doing this for if I'm running myself into the ground. The company, all of it. What's it for.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me see if I can pull together what I'm hearing. You came back today — partly because Sarah asked, but also because something in you wasn't ready to dismiss this entirely. The lab results unsettled you more than you let on. Seeing Sarah cry got to a part of you that logic couldn't quite reach. And now, for the first time, you're connecting some of these dots — your age, your father, what 'later' might actually cost you. And you're asking yourself what you're doing this all for. That's... a lot to be sitting with.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. That's... yeah, that's it. I've spent thirty years being the guy who fixes things. I don't — I'm not good at being the thing that needs fixing. But maybe I've been fixing all the wrong things. I don't know. Maybe.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Maybe fixing the wrong things. That's worth sitting with. And I just want to say — getting to that place, saying that out loud, that took something real.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It did. I'm not — I'm not making any grand promises here. That's not me. But I think... I actually think I want to figure this out. Not for Sarah, not for the doctor. For me. I think I want to.

client_context: A 20-year-old star athlete whose performance has been slipping due to partying. Coach gave an ultimatum. Torn between team loyalty and social life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in... take whatever seat feels right. I'm glad you made it. I know these rooms can feel kind of strange, especially the first time. There's nothing you have to do here today — no checklist, nothing you have to prove. I'm just wondering, how are you doing right now, walking in here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I'm here. That's about all I can say, I guess. Coach kind of made it real clear this wasn't optional, so. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So this feels like something that was handed to you. Not a door you opened yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Pretty much. I mean, I don't — I don't think I have like a problem or whatever. My whole team drinks, everyone does. It's just... last semester things got a little out of hand and now suddenly it's this whole thing. My coach is treating me like I'm some kind of, I don't know. It's just a lot of drama for what it is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Before any of this — the ultimatum, coming here — what was this season supposed to look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was gonna be... this was supposed to be my year. Like, I've been working toward starting since freshman year. Two years of scout team, special teams, all of it. And this season was finally it. And I just... I don't know what happened, honestly. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something you'd been building toward for years. And now it feels like it's... slipping through your hands.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My dad drove, like, four hours to watch me play last month. And I had maybe twenty minutes of real game time. I was hungover. I didn't — I didn't tell him that. He still thinks everything's great, I'm crushing it. And I just stood there after the game smiling for pictures and I felt like... I don't know. Like the worst person. I don't know why I'm even telling you that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took something to say out loud. Carrying all of that — standing there smiling, your dad right next to you — and no one knowing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
...

Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does the drinking give you? Like, when you think about why it happens — what is it doing for you in those moments?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's the only time I can like... turn everything off. During the season it's just nonstop — film, practice, class, coaches watching every little thing, your teammates depending on you. At a party you're just a guy. Nobody's looking at you expecting something. You can just exist without it meaning anything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's the one place where you don't have to be the athlete. Where no one needs anything from you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: But even that's not... it's not really working anymore. Because I wake up the next morning and I just feel worse. And then it's harder to practice, and I feel like I'm letting everybody down, and then I want to go out again just to not feel that. It's like this loop. I didn't actually — I hadn't really seen it that clearly until just now. That's kind of messed up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The version of you that put in two years on scout team, that your dad drove four hours for — what does he want? Not what your coach wants, not what I want. What does that guy actually want for himself?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
He wants to play. Like, actually play. He wants to earn that starting spot for real, not just have it handed to him because someone else got hurt. He wants to be good again.

...

I miss it. I actually miss just being good at something. That's — I haven't said that to anyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That guy is still in there. You just described him like he's real, like he's worth something. Like he's worth fighting for.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I never thought about it like that. Like I'm fighting for him. That's a weird way to think about yourself. But yeah. Yeah, I think... something needs to change. I don't know exactly what that looks like yet. But I can see it now. I can see that it does.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in today because you had to. And somewhere in the middle of this conversation, you started talking about a guy who loves the game, who didn't want to let his dad down, who's caught in a loop he can now see clearly. That's not a small thing. That's real clarity. So I want to ask — of everything we've touched today, what's the one thing you want to hold onto when you walk out of here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
Just... that I still care. About the game. I think I've been numbing everything out for so long I kind of forgot that I actually love playing. Like that's still real. That's still a thing.

(small laugh)

That probably sounds dumb.

client_context: A 40-year-old single parent who has been drinking a bottle of wine nightly to cope with the stress of raising two kids alone. Knows it's too much but feels trapped.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know this probably wasn't how you planned to spend your afternoon. What's on your mind as we're getting started?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I don't want to be here. My boss basically said come or else, so. Here I am. I'm not — I want to be clear right off the bat — I'm not an alcoholic. I don't have a drinking problem. I have a stress problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You were backed into a corner on this. And that's a lousy way to walk into any room.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. I'm a forty-year-old woman, I raise two kids by myself, I go to work every single day — and suddenly I'm being sent to... counseling? Like I'm some kind of liability. It's insulting. It is genuinely insulting.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Being judged by your employer — especially when you're giving everything you have — that stings in a particular way. Can you tell me what happened at work, from your side of it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I was late twice. Twice. And apparently I — quote — 'seemed off' one morning. My youngest was sick, I was up until like 3am, I barely slept. That's not a drinking problem, that's just... that's just life when you're doing it completely alone. Nobody seems to understand that part.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're carrying an enormous amount. Everything lands on you — sick kids in the middle of the night, work the next morning, all of it. And you still show up.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. I do. Because nobody else is going to. But I — look, I'm not drinking at work, I want to be really clear about that. I have wine at night to unwind. A bottle, maybe, but that's... after a day like mine, I think that's pretty understandable.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me more about the unwinding. Walk me through what the end of your day actually looks like.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's just... chaotic. Come home, make dinner, help with homework, try to get them both settled. By the time I actually sit down it's like nine, ten at night. And I'm just done. Like completely emptied out. The wine is the only thing that actually turns my brain off. Otherwise I'd just lay there staring at the ceiling thinking about everything I didn't get done.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's the one thing at the end of the day that actually belongs to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. Yeah, that's — I never thought about it that way but. Yeah. After everyone gets what they need from me, that's... that's mine. That's the only quiet I get. Is that — I mean, is that so bad?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you're running on empty most days, doing it completely alone, and the wine has become the thing that refuels you — even just enough to get through to tomorrow. And part of what makes being here so hard is it feels like someone's trying to take away the only thing that's yours.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...When you put it like that. I don't know. Maybe. I just — okay, I know a bottle is a lot. I'm not stupid. I've Googled it. I know what it says. I just don't — I genuinely don't know what else I would do instead. That's the honest answer.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Saying that out loud — especially the first time, to a stranger — that takes something. I want to ask you something, and you don't have to have a neat answer. What would it mean for your kids if things stayed exactly the same from here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: God. I don't — I hate that question. My older one, she's twelve, she's sharp. She asked me once why the recycling always has so many wine bottles. I just said we recycle a lot of stuff. But she has this look. Like she's doing math in her head and she already knows the answer.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She sees you. And you see her seeing you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And that — that's actually what scares me. Not my job, not any of this. It's her. I don't want her to look back someday and think that I... I don't want to be that story for her. She deserves better than that story.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So underneath everything — the frustration about being sent here, the exhaustion, the wine at the end of the night — there's a mother who is genuinely terrified of failing her daughter. That's not a small thing to sit with. What would you want things to look like, even just a little differently?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know yet. I really don't. But... I think maybe I needed to say some of this out loud. I haven't said any of it out loud before. To anyone.

client_context: A 38-year-old mandated by court to attend counseling after a second DUI. Furious about being forced to be here. Sees the system as unfair.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came back. I'll be honest — I wasn't a hundred percent sure you would. So, what's on your mind walking in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: What's on my mind. [laughs bitterly] Look, I'm here because my probation officer said I had to be. Full stop. I don't think I have some... condition. I just need to get through these sessions, get my license back, and get on with my life. So whatever you need to check off the list, let's check it off and be done.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Get your life back. That's the goal. And you showed up — even though this is probably the last place you want to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well. I'm not gonna throw away my custody situation over this. My kids need me around. That's the only reason I walked back in here. But yeah. I came back.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your kids keep coming up. What's this whole situation — the arrest, the court, all of it — what's it actually doing to your relationship with them?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My ex is dragging it into the custody hearing. Every single thing, she's like, 'he's irresponsible, he can't be trusted with the kids.' And my son — he's twelve — he asked me straight up why I got arrested. I didn't know what to... I mean, what do you even say to that? But none of that is because I'm some drunk. It's because the system is stacked against guys like me. Two beers, barely over the limit, and I'm treated like a criminal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your son looking at you differently — that sounds like it cuts a lot deeper than anything the court is throwing at you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Obviously. I'm his dad. I don't want him thinking I'm some kind of — [trails off] It just got blown way out of proportion. That's all I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Even underneath all the anger at the courts, at your ex — being the dad your son can look up to, that's what you keep circling back to.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Of course. But nobody in that courtroom gives a damn about any of that. I'm just a case number. I show up, pay my fines, do my sessions — and meanwhile my ex gets to rewrite history and I'm supposed to, what, sit here and pick apart every beer I've ever had? I know my limits. I drive a truck for a living. I'm not an idiot.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I hear you. Let me ask you something different — a year from now, if things were actually going the way you wanted them to, what does that look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: A year from now. [long pause] I'd have my full license back. My kids would be at my place on weekends, not just these supervised visits. I'd be... [quieter] I don't know. Honestly? I haven't thought that far ahead in a while. It's just been — just trying not to screw up the next thing in front of me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Just surviving the next thing. That's a heavy way to live.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: [quiet] Yeah. I mean... I used to have plans. Was gonna save up, buy a piece of land upstate — my dad had some property out there and I always thought maybe someday I'd... [stops himself] It's stupid. I don't know why I'm even bringing that up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's not stupid. That's you telling me who you are when you strip all the court stuff away. The guy with plans for land upstate — he didn't disappear.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: [long pause] ... I've been drinking more since the divorce. I know that. I'm not gonna sit here and pretend I don't know that. Coming home to an empty apartment, it's — you have a couple beers, it gets quieter in your head, you know? I'm not saying it's a problem. But it's more than it used to be. I'll give you that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me make sure I'm hearing you right. You came back today — and I don't think it's only about the PO. Your kids are at the center of all of this for you. You've got plans and dreams that got pushed aside somewhere along the way. And you're telling me the drinking has picked up, especially when you're alone in that apartment at night. That's a lot to be sitting with.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: [exhales slowly] When you put it like that... yeah. I didn't think I'd end up here. Two DUIs. That's not — that's not who I thought I was gonna be. [pause] I actually want things to be different. For my kids, at least. I do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You want things to be different. What's one small thing — something realistic, something you could actually picture yourself doing — that moves you even a little bit toward that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've been thinking about not keeping beer in the apartment. Like... if it's not just sitting there in the fridge, I don't have to make that decision every single night. That probably sounds dumb. But it's something. Maybe I can try that.

client_context: An 18-year-old referred by school counselor after being caught drinking at a school event. Feels singled out since 'literally everyone drinks'.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in. I'm Dr. Marcus — or just Marcus, whatever works for you. Fair warning, this place looks like every other clinic room you've probably been dragged into, but I promise I'm slightly more interesting than the beige walls. So... court sent you. That's not exactly the fun way to end up here, huh?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well, I didn't exactly volunteer. Can we just... get this over with? I have stuff to do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Totally fair. Before we figure out what 'getting this over with' even looks like — what's your take on what happened? Like, from your perspective. Not the paperwork version.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My perspective? Okay so — I was at a party after the game, literally everyone was drinking, and I got singled out because I guess someone didn't like me or whatever. It's so stupid. I shouldn't even be here right now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you got pulled out of a crowd doing the exact same thing, and now you're the one sitting in a clinic.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly! Like, why me? My friends were drinking way more than I was and nobody said a single thing to them. Not one word. It's not fair.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That is genuinely frustrating — and honestly? Showing up here when you clearly didn't want to, that actually takes something. I want to ask you though — and you don't have to have a great answer — is it all just bad luck? Or is there any part of you that's been sitting with this at all?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I don't know. Maybe. But I wasn't even that drunk. Like, I had a couple drinks. It's not like I was falling over or anything. My friend Kaya had way more than me and she's totally fine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So in your world, what happened that night was just... normal. Like, this is what people do.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah? Like everyone I know drinks. It's not a big deal. My older sister drinks. My parents have wine at dinner literally every night. I don't get why it's suddenly this massive thing when I do it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm. The rules feel like they apply differently to you than to everyone around you. That's a heavy thing to carry.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... I mean, I don't know. I guess. It just feels like — ugh, I don't even know how to explain it. Like I'm always getting watched or something. It's just... exhausting.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Always feeling like you're under a microscope — that wears on a person. What's actually at stake for you here, do you think? Like, what does this whole situation actually threaten for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just... I try not to think about it too much. But sometimes I wonder if like... I don't know. What if this messes up my college applications? I applied to a couple schools and if they find out about this... I don't know. That actually kind of scares me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Even sitting here angry, you're already thinking about what comes next. That's not nothing. Sounds like there are things you've actually worked for that you don't want to lose.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. I worked really hard for my grades. Like, really hard. I don't want to throw all of that away over something that felt like nothing at the time. I just... I didn't think. I didn't think about any of it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me pull together what I'm hearing, because there's actually a lot here. You came in angry — and that makes sense. You felt singled out for doing something everyone around you does, and that unfairness is real. And at the same time, I'm also hearing someone who has worked hard, who has real goals, and who's starting to notice that this could actually cost her something she cares about. Does that feel close to it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...yeah. Yeah, that's kind of it, actually. I don't know, I've never really said it out loud before. It sounds different when someone else says it back to you.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So thinking about where you go from here — not what the court needs, not what I need — what would actually feel right to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know exactly... but like... I don't want to be back here again. No offense. I just — I actually want to go to college. I want that. So maybe I need to be smarter about, like... where I am and what I'm doing. I don't know. Maybe.
